Breaking: Apple TV 4K review: The best streamer comes at a cost

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here.
  • Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.
  • Industry observers note that the Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s been four years since Apple last updated the Apple TV 4K, but a new version is here. There’s Siri AI support, a faster chip, an improved remote, and more.

Here’s everything that’s changed, what’s better, and whether the new Apple TV 4K justifies its new $299 price.

Industry observers note that the Apple TV 4K’s overall design is largely unchanged. It’s still the same familiar black box that sits underneath your television. The only visual change is that the front status light has moved from the right side to the center.

Inside, Apple has upgraded the A15 Bionic to the A19 chip, touting 50% faster CPU performance and twice the GPU performance.

Those are great improvements on paper. In practice, I’m not doing anything on my Apple TV that really stresses the performance. Compared to my third-generation Apple TV 4K, I’ve occasionally noticed slightly smoother animations and faster performance in apps that handle more processing locally, like Infuse.

According to recent reports, I think the biggest advantage of the A19 chip is future-proofing. People tend to buy and keep these devices for years. In fact, I’m still using a first-generation Apple TV 4K from 2017 in my bedroom, and it still works just fine nearly a decade later. The A19 gives the fresh Apple TV plenty of performance headroom for future tvOS updates and more demanding apps, even if those advantages aren’t particularly noticeable today.

The Siri Remote looks the same as before, but it now supports Precision Finding in the Find My app, making it easier to track down when misplaced. You can also play a sound on the remote to help locate it. I lose my Siri Remote all the time, so this honestly might be the change I’ve noticed and appreciated most in my 10 days testing the latest Apple TV.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting Apple also sells the fresh Siri Remote separately for $59, and it’s compatible with every previous Apple TV 4K generation. You do, however, need a newer iPhone model to use Precision Finding.

According to recent reports, one of the more interesting new features is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room. Apple TV automatically calibrates the speakers based on their positions in the room.

Industry observers note that for context, I typically use my Apple TV with a stereo pair of full-size HomePod (2nd generation) speakers. I’ve spent some time testing the newly introduced four-speaker surround sound setup by adding a pair of HomePod mini 2 speakers.

My house’s layout isn’t particularly well-suited for a traditional surround sound setup, but to my admittedly untrained ears, this sounds great. I can’t speak to how it compares to a dedicated surround sound system, but I appreciate Apple continuing to expand what’s possible with HomePods and Apple TV.

One of the biggest changes with the upcoming Apple TV 4K is the addition of three far-field microphones. This means you can now interact with Siri without picking up the Siri Remote. In conjunction with this, Siri AI is also coming to Apple TV.

Siri AI brings the same broad world knowledge and personal-context capabilities you’ve experienced on iPhone and HomeView, but adapts them to finding and watching content on your television. Siri AI on Apple TV requires the owner of your Apple Home setup to have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Personal context requests also require a paired compatible device connected to the same Wi-Fi network as Apple TV.

What movie did Zac recommend I watch?

What was that TV show Lily recommended a few weeks ago?

What are some baseball movies I might like?

What did the vet say after Blake’s vet appointment?

For each example, tvOS responded with a dedicated interface on Apple TV, showing the answer along with poster art, cast information, and more. It also offers built-in contextual suggestions when you ask for recommendations, so you can refine the results further.

You can also ask Siri contextual questions about the show or movie you’re watching. This includes things like “where was this show filmed?” and “when is the next season coming out?”.

I’ve found Siri AI’s responses to those contextual questions less accurate. It struggles to accurately identify the show or movie that’s playing, leading to completely inaccurate responses to those types of questions.

It has been revealed that it’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021 and the third-generation model from 2022. The far-field microphones are what’s exclusive to the new hardware. This lets you shout Siri commands into the air without talking directly into the Siri Remote.

In my testing, hands-free Siri works relatively well, and it’s convenient to control Apple TV without reaching for the remote. It does a good job at picking up commands.

Industry observers note that I can’t go any further in this review without talking about the price. The Apple TV 4K (4th generation) costs $299. That’s a huge increase over previous Apple TV models. Here’s a brief history of Apple TV 4K pricing over the years to set the stage:.

After Apple introduced the $129 Apple TV model in October 2022, I started to notice a change. More and more people had Apple TVs when I would visit. Friends and family who had previously bought an Amazon or Roku box, or just used their TV’s built-in software, had purchased an Apple TV.

In a recent development, at $299, I worry that type of adoption is going to come to a screeching halt. And it’s unfortunate because the Apple TV is so much better than anything else out there. tvOS is fast, clean, and relatively free of the clutter and advertisements you find on competing platforms. The Siri Remote is excellent, and the integration with the rest of Apple’s ecosystem is hard to beat.

In a recent development, I could justify the $299 price for the Apple TV 4K (4th generation) if it were just one option available in a broader lineup. If there were lower-priced options for people who don’t need all the bells and whistles. That’s not the case, though. In fact, this is the first Apple TV 4K generation to be sold in just one configuration. There’s no cheaper version with less storage or fewer features.

Recent findings suggest that to Apple’s credit, these are devices that can last for years. The fact that I’m still using an Apple TV 4K from 2017 makes the $299 price a tiny bit easier to swallow, but it doesn’t really change my frustration.

Apple seems serious about its upcoming smart home strategy. There’s the HomeView smart display, a new HomePod mini, and the Apple Home Collection family of smart home accessories launching later this year. One of the best ways to get deeper into people’s homes is by controlling how they watch TV. I can’t help but think pricing the Apple TV 4K out of reach for so many people will hinder those ambitions.

Recent findings suggest that don’t get me wrong, I love the Apple TV. I have three of them in my house. If one of them broke, I would reluctantly pay $299 for a newly introduced one. Whether you fall into that category is for you to decide. All I can say is that the new Apple TV 4K is the best streamer on the market.

Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cornell

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time, researchers can track the movement of a person’s entire body with ultrasonic sound waves, using just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model – all while ensuring privacy and efficiency.
  • The latest technology, called EchoMotion, was developed by Cornell’s Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab, directed by Cheng Zhang, associate professor of information science in the Cornell Ann S.
  • EchoMotion represents a scalable approach that can use AI to understand human behaviors in the real world, Zheng noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time, researchers can track the movement of a person’s entire body with ultrasonic sound waves, using just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model – all while ensuring privacy and efficiency.

The latest technology, called EchoMotion, was developed by Cornell’s Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab, directed by Cheng Zhang, associate professor of information science in the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. It uses the built-in speaker and microphone on a commercial smartwatch to determine a person’s body position using a sonar-like sensing system. Once EchoMotion is integrated into commercial wearables or virtual reality (VR) systems, it could be used for tracking workouts, daily activities and progress on physical rehabilitation.

EchoMotion represents a scalable approach that can use AI to understand human behaviors in the real world, Zheng noted.

He presented the paper, “EchoMotion: Towards Full-Body Pose Tracking with a Single Smartwatch Using Active Acoustic Sensing,” at the Association for Computing Machinery international joint conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing and International Symposium on Wearable Computing (UbiComp/IWSC), Oct. 13 in Shanghai.

Saif Mahmud, a Ph.D. candidate in the field of information science, demonstrates EchoMotion, a system for tracking body movements using an off-the-shelf smartwatch.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a very important jump for body tracking,” mentioned Saif Mahmud, doctoral student in the field of information science and lead author of the newly introduced research. Existing wearable devices use sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes that determine the movement of the device alone, he said. As a result, whole body tracking traditionally has required more complicated setups that may also include smartphones, earbuds or VR headsets.

Some tracking systems also integrate cameras, but EchoMotion’s use of sound waves offers multiple advantages. Acoustic signals preserve privacy for the wearer and the people around them – no need to set up a camera at the gym – and generate smaller amounts of data for easier and cheaper processing.

“While large language models, like ChatGPT, have been in the news, EchoMotion shows how very small models running on wearables have also revolutionized sensing in human-computer interaction,” mentioned co-author François Guimbretière, professor of information science in Cornell Bowers.

According to recent reports, the technology also saves on battery power and works with existing off-the-shelf watches. In the prototype, sensing drew about 12 milliwatts, roughly 40 times less than a wearable camera, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used only 5% to 6% of the battery.

“We have made significant efforts in making EchoMotion work on commercial devices, so that the adoption can be very easy,” Mahmud said.

To develop the technology, the researchers initially created their own 3D-printed watch replica, which included a microphone and speaker pair on each side. The two speakers emit ultrasonic signals that surround a person in a sphere of inaudible sound waves. Then the two microphones pick up the echoes that bounce off the person’s limbs as they move.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers collected echo patterns from 10 volunteers who wore the watch on their nondominant hand as they performed 18 exercises. Using that data, the researchers developed a deep learning model to translate those patterns into body movements. They measured accuracy by comparing the predicted positions of 12 joints, from head to ankles, with the body poses captured by cameras.

Sources indicate that off-the-shelf smartwatches have only a single microphone and speaker pair, however, so they tested the EchoMotion system on an unmodified Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 with 15 new volunteers. When used by people new to the system, the average error for predicting the location of each joint was under four inches. A one-time, 12-minute calibration cut that error by more than one third, to about 2.4 inches.

The same AI model, without any retraining, also worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3.

According to recent reports, to see how EchoMotion performed beyond the lab, the researchers asked 10 new participants to wear a smartwatch as they did the 18 exercises in a small room, in a narrow hallway and next to a noisy road. Furniture and ambient noise did not interfere, but the system’s performance suffered slightly in the hallway, due to echoes coming off of other people. Mahmud expects, however, that with more data – from thousands of users instead of dozens – their model will get better at interpreting a wearer’s movements even in crowded environments, like the subway.

According to recent reports, currently, the team is developing the technology for use in fitness tracking, so a personal fitness agent will be able to count a user’s reps and even correct their form, for example, in a Bulgarian split squat. They are also exploring the use of EchoMotion in combination with first-person vision on smartglasses to efficiently track the objects that a person handles.

“In the very near future, with wearables like smartwatches or smartglasses, a personal agent will write a description of your whole day – what you did, what you ate,” Mahmud said. “This project enables the body tracking part of that vision.”.

Co-authors on the study include Jiwan Kim of KAIST; Tianhong Catherine Yu, a doctoral student in the field of information science; Kenny Liang ’24 and Vineet Parikh ’20, M.S. ’24.

The research was supported by the National Science Foundation.

In a recent development, patricia Waldron is a writer for the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science.

#4032. Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple HomeView review: An adorable smart display that earns its place

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s HomeView smart display is here.
  • Industry observers note that I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen.
  • Recent findings suggest that homeView is an adorable little thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s HomeView smart display is here. It combines a 7-inch display with Siri AI and an all-new software experience that actually feels really familiar.

Industry observers note that I’ve spent the last ten days living with HomeView in my kitchen. Here’s everything you need to know.

Recent findings suggest that homeView is an adorable little thing. That’s the best way to describe it. A 7-inch square display sits atop a rounded aluminum speaker base. A small, polished metal arm connects it and lets you tilt the display forward and backward.

In a recent development, homeView comes in four colors: Starlight, Rose Pink, Silver, and Space Gray. My review unit is Starlight, and it’s very subtle. I had to double-check the box to make sure it was Starlight, not Silver.

The decision to make the display square is interesting. Between that design and the software experience centered around faces and widgets, HomeView really does feel like an oversized Apple Watch for your home.

Recent findings suggest that I really appreciate the square display. It makes HomeView look less like an iPad propped up on a stand and more like a dedicated, purpose-driven device.

It has been revealed that in terms of specs, the 7-inch display has a 1088 × 1088 resolution, equating to a pixel density of 220 pixels per inch. Max brightness is 500 nits. It can also dim all the way to 0.3 nits, which means it can go in a bedroom without being a nuisance. It also has True Tone to match your room’s lighting temperature.

For the past ten days, my partner and I have been living with HomeView on our kitchen counter. The square display and aluminum base look great in that setting. I don’t think an iPad-style display would look nearly as intentional. We also don’t have much spare counter space. If HomeView were any bigger or wider, I’m not sure we’d have room for it.

In the lead-up to HomeView’s launch, I was skeptical of how usable a 7-inch display would be. In practice, I’ve found this to be (mostly) a non-matter. Apple has done a great job optimizing the interface for the display. Text is readable at a glance from a few feet away, timers are nice and large, and the interface adapts to show more information when you’re closer.

Sometimes I wish it were bigger. Viewing a recipe requires a bit more scrolling than I would like. It’d be nice to fit a couple more widgets on the Modular face. But those trade-offs are easier to accept when I consider how much I appreciate HomeView’s compact footprint.

Recent findings suggest that apple touts that the HomeView has a custom-engineered acoustic system. There are two custom full-range drivers in the display, paired with a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators in the base.

Industry observers note that in practice, HomeView’s sound quality falls somewhere between the HomePod mini and the full-size second-generation HomePod. Its sound quality won’t blow you away, but it’s respectable for music and podcast playback. I replaced a full-size original HomePod in my kitchen with it, and while it doesn’t sound quite as good, it makes up for it in other ways … like by having a screen.

Recent findings suggest that homeView can serve as an AirPlay target, too, so you can beam content from your iPhone or other Apple device right to it. You can also AirPlay from HomeView to other AirPlay targets in your house.

HomeView doesn’t have any buttons, which is a design decision I’ve found very frustrating on multiple occasions. I wish it had volume buttons, so I could rapidly adjust the volume without yelling at Siri or using the touchscreen.

HomeView’s software borrows heavily from iOS and watchOS. The interface is built around a system of faces with widgets, very similar to the Apple Watch’s complications system. The process of configuring a face will feel very familiar to Apple Watch and iPhone consumers.

You can customize faces by long-pressing on them, which reveals a familiar “Customize” screen. Here, you can change the style, color, widgets, and background. You can also add widgets from your nearby iPhone. Apple states that widgets are visible to everyone, but widget content is only visible while your primary device is in the home.

According to recent reports, I’ve become particularly fond of the Modular face, which lets you place four equally sized square widgets. I think it provides a nice amount of glanceable information without feeling too dense. The Photos face is also a delight, essentially turning the HomeView into a digital picture frame. Support for Shared Albums is especially nice.

It has been revealed that I think Apple made the right decision by building the HomeView experience around faces rather than a traditional app-focused interface. Most of the time, HomeView is just sitting on your counter or table, and you’re not actively interacting with it. That’s why I’ve gravitated towards the Modular face.

Industry observers note that the faces system also means that HomeView doesn’t constantly draw your attention. Just like the physical design, it’s there when you need it, but otherwise does a good job blending into the background.

Swiping down from the left two-thirds of the display activates Siri AI, while swiping down from the top right takes you to Control Center (which annoyingly isn’t customizable). Swiping up from the bottom takes you to the Home Screen, where you’ll find a grid of apps and spots to add even more widgets.

According to recent reports, there is no App Store on HomeView. Instead, there’s a collection of built-in Apple apps paired with audio and video apps through its CarPlay-based app system. Here are the Apple apps that are available on HomeView:.

Recent findings suggest that I’m hopeful that Apple builds on the app story for HomeView sooner rather than later. I don’t think HomeView needs its own App Store, but I do think it needs more apps. This includes more Apple apps and additional third-party apps.

I desperately want Apple to add the Notes app to HomeView. My wife and I keep recipes and dinner ideas in Notes, so it would be great to have that experience available on HomeView. It feels like an odd omission right now. HomeView also needs a dedicated Photos app.

I think the idea of basing the system on CarPlay makes sense. There are a lot of similarities in UI between how an app should work in the car and on a smart display. The Audible app, for example, translates really well from CarPlay to HomeView, as does Spotify.

Recent findings suggest that however, the list of supported categories for CarPlay is a lot broader than the audio and video category Apple is allowing on HomeView right now. There are signs this could expand very soon, and I’m hopeful that’s the case.

It has been revealed that one of the cleverest aspects of HomeView is its recipe experience. When you open a recipe in Safari, HomeView gives you the option to convert it into a dedicated cooking interface. You can browse for recipes directly on HomeView, or find one on your iPhone and simply hold it in front of HomeView to hand off the webpage.

Sources indicate that homeView then intelligently detects the actual recipe information and puts it into a streamlined interface. You can view the full ingredient list and measurements, and check off items as you go. The recipe itself is broken down into individual steps. It also intelligently identifies when you need to set a timer and gives you the option to start one directly from the recipe.

This is the exact type of feature that’s perfect for HomeView, and perfect for a dedicated screen sitting on the kitchen counter. You don’t have to keep reaching for your phone, unlocking it, and finding your place in the recipe.

According to recent reports, the feature works incredibly well. I tried it with recipes of varying lengths from multiple different websites without any major problems.

In a recent development, there are some limitations, though. For example, it does struggle if a website splits the recipe into multiple pages. Also, as I mentioned earlier, the 7-inch display means there’s more scrolling involved than I’d like. It doesn’t solve my frustration with the lack of a dedicated Notes app. Still, it’s a great example of where this design excels.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the HomeView’s software interface is really well done. Delightful animations appear throughout the experience, like when notifications or the Siri blob slide in from the top bezel. Everything feels very smooth. The software feels familiar because of its similarities to Apple Watch and iPhone, but it’s also clearly purpose-built for the smart display form factor.

Since HomeView is meant for everyone in your home, Apple had to engineer a multi-user system. HomeView supports up to six people, each with their own personalized Home Screen, widgets, and access to personal information.

Industry observers note that homeView identifies the different people in your house in two ways: facial recognition and voice recognition. The goal is to recognize who’s interacting with it and customize the experience for that person. So, when I approach HomeView, it can recognize my face and display my calendar, reminders, and messages. When my wife approaches, it can recognize her instead and show her information.

In a recent development, the facial recognition implementation is particularly interesting. HomeView doesn’t have Face ID. Instead, it uses its built-in camera for facial recognition. During setup, you’re asked to turn your head left, right, up, and down so HomeView can capture your face from different angles.

Recent findings suggest that in practice, HomeView’s facial recognition works surprisingly well. I was skeptical, but it’s done a good job of identifying both my wife and me. If I approach it and try to open the Messages app while it’s on my wife’s profile, I get a message saying it can’t verify my identity. If I repeatedly try, HomeView disables facial recognition, requiring my wife to authenticate using her iPhone before she can access her personal information again.

In addition to protecting personal data, HomeView does a decent job of automatically switching between profiles. There’s occasionally a delay of a few seconds, so I wish it were slightly faster.

In a recent development, homeView is powered by Apple’s A18 chip, which enables support for Siri AI. However, Siri AI works a bit differently on HomeView than on other Apple devices.

Recent findings suggest that homeView can answer world knowledge questions on its own, without relying on a paired iPhone or iPad. This is basically the trivia questions we’ve all grown accustomed to shouting at voice assistants over the years. The difference, of course, is that Siri AI answers these questions well, unlike old Siri. On HomeView, the experience is even better because you can visually see the response on the display, often accompanied by images or other visual information.

The second aspect of Siri AI is personal context. To use Siri AI’s personal context on HomeView, you need an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad in your house.

Apple says that the device must have been recently unlocked and be connected to the same Wi-Fi network as HomeView.

In my testing over the last 10 days, I’ve never run into a situation where HomeView was unable to answer a Siri AI query because my iPhone was unavailable.

It has been revealed that I’ve found Siri AI to be quite impressive and useful since it debuted in September. It’s a huge upgrade over old Siri. Broadly speaking, that experience extends to HomeView.

Industry observers note that many of the same personal context questions I ask on my iPhone can now be answered by HomeView. And because of HomeView’s form factor, it’s more useful when multitasking. Instead of reaching for my iPhone or hoping it’s within earshot, I can just ask HomeView.

Here are a few questions HomeView has answered without a hiccup:.

In terms of speed, I’ve found HomeView to be slightly slower to answer personal context questions than my iPhone Duo. It’s not a huge difference, but it’s a few seconds each time. I assume this is because HomeView is basically handing off the request to my iPhone, adding an additional step that requests directly on the iPhone don’t have to do.

In a recent development, siri AI is not without its faults. There are times on HomeView where it just hangs and never responds, or responds with a generic “Sorry, try again later” message of some sort. HomeView’s primary interaction method is your voice, which makes these types of Siri AI failures even more frustrating.

It has been revealed that homeView can also serve as the command center for your smart home. It has a dedicated Home app, as well as multiple different Home-focused face options. You can also, of course, use your voice to control HomeKit accessories and scenes through Siri.

There’s ultimately nothing particularly remarkable about HomeView’s support for smart home control. It offers much of the same functionality as the Home app on your iPhone, but in one central location that everyone in your house can use.

There is one limitation: you at the moment can’t use Siri AI on HomeView to control secure devices like locks and garage doors, even if the device recognizes you. If they are part of a scene, you can tell Siri AI to set the scene and it works. But you can’t individually control them.

Apple tells Joanna Stern that a software revision coming next month will add security accessory support to HomeView’s Siri AI.

I wish Apple would expand what HomeView can do for the smart home. It has a built-in camera, so why can’t I use that camera for motion sensing or as a HomeKit Secure Video camera?

I’ve found the screen most useful for promptly checking the status of accessories, like seeing whether a door is locked or glancing at the doorbell camera. For actually controlling accessories, I still find Siri and automations to be the easiest approach. HomeView hasn’t really changed that, although I do appreciate being able to adjust the thermostat right from the kitchen counter.

HomeView costs $299, which is about $100 less than I expected based on rumors. That’s a surprisingly reasonable price, I think. The key, of course, is whether you’ll actually use it day to day.

According to recent reports, when you get a fresh iPhone, you already have a pretty good idea of what you’ll use it for and where it fits into your life. New features might change how you use it, but the core functionality stays the same.

According to recent reports, homeView is very different. At first, it sits on your counter and is nice to look at. It’s a very, very cute little thing. But it takes time to discover how and why it fits into your life.

At first, I had no idea whether I’d actually use HomeView. But in the ten days it’s been sitting on my counter, it’s grown on me quite a bit. It’s gone from being a nice-to-have to something I use and rely on for multiple tasks each day.

In a recent development, it’s also been interesting watching my partner interact with it. Her first impression was essentially, “It’s cute, but I don’t know what I’ll use it for.” Over the last week, however, she’s remarked multiple times how much she likes it.

Whether it’s personal context-focused Siri AI interactions, simply being able to glance and see how long is left on a timer, watching the animated album art as a song plays, or the joy of the Photos face, HomeView has earned its spot.

Sources indicate that in fact, I moved HomeView from our kitchen to my office for a day to test a few features and settings in more depth. While cooking dinner that night, we both found ourselves shouting Siri commands into the air and glancing at the empty spot on the counter, only to remember it wasn’t there.

Sources indicate that I think that’s the best example of what makes HomeView special. You don’t have to be a HomeKit enthusiast or spend hours tinkering with smart home automations to appreciate it. It’s a device everyone in the house can find their own uses for, and it becomes more useful the longer it’s part of your routine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google today declared Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20.

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

In a recent development, on the privacy front, there is a blinking white indicator light when you use the camera to take pictures or record clips that are saved to your library. If the light is covered or disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Android XR running a hardware check when charging.

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Recent findings suggest that other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

A 3D illustration of the Google logo.

Google has released AdMob agent skills that let AI coding agents, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, add and check ad code in mobile apps. A Gemini-built assistant, Ask AdMob, and an MCP server that lets agents manage AdMob accounts are still in testing, with more agent tools planned for 2027.

It has been revealed that google is adding AI tools to AdMob, its service for showing ads inside mobile apps, the organization declared on Monday. The one available now lets developers hand ad setup to AI coding agents, including rival tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. The rest is still in testing.

The upcoming “agent skills” are ready-made instructions that teach an AI agent how to work with Google’s ad code. Developers can ask it to add banner or full-screen ads, move to Google’s newest ads toolkit, or check an app for setup errors before launch. Google says this replaces clicking through dashboards and copying ad IDs by hand.

Recent findings suggest that google is also building an MCP server, a link that would let agents read AdMob account data, create ad slots and change settings. It is in early testing and should reach more developers early next year. Developers will have to approve changes before they go live.

Sources indicate that the second tool, Ask AdMob, is a chat assistant built with Gemini that sits inside a developer’s AdMob account. Google claims it will flag setup problems, suggest ad networks that could earn more, and catch typos in pricing settings. Developers can also set brand safety rules in plain language instead of keeping block lists.

It has been revealed that testing of Ask AdMob starts over the next few months. Google plans features that act on a user’s behalf later in 2027, but says every suggestion will still need approval.

According to recent reports, supporting outside agents fits a wider industry shift. In August, OpenAI and four rivals agreed on one standard for agent skills and MCP servers. IronSource’s founders, who sold their app ad company for $4.4B, are betting AI agents will replace ad buyers altogether.

For Google, keeping app makers on its ad network matters, as Meta is set to overtake it as the world’s biggest ad manufacturer this year.
