📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that golden Board is a binary message designed to teach chess to an unknown recipient without a shared language, culture, or prior knowledge of the game. It begins by teaching the format needed to read its own contents.

The full project code and documentation are available on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that this guide follows that process: recover numbers from the bits, use them to reconstruct pictures and interactions, then learn how those pictures describe chess. One complete game connects the layers, from its physical bits to its final displayed position.

Before we dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things about the project.

Sources indicate that in a nutshell, Golden Board is a sequence of 4,194,304 bits, or 512 KiB of ones and zeros. That number suggests arranging them into a 2,048 × 2,048 square.

Recent findings suggest that the first 64 rows contain 32 drawings, each 64 × 64 cells. Together they form the bootstrap: it teaches how to read the rest of the message. It's chess-agnostic and can be used to decode other structured messages.

The payload below contains visual chess lessons, exercises with feedback, complete games, and the information needed to find, check and display them.

I took inspiration from messages intended for unknown intelligences, such as the Voyager Golden Record, Lincos, and others.

But instead of sharing scientific knowledge or works of art, Golden Board teaches chess.

First, a small set of rules opens up an enormous world of possibilities, ideas and beauty.

Second, a game can share more than knowledge: it offers a glimpse of the human mind.

I ran trials using LLMs as stand-ins for unknown recipients, testing decoding and understanding with raw bits, decoded content, and varying levels of assistance.

In a recent development, correctly recovering the bytes and understanding the lessons are separate tests. These models already know chess, so correct chess answers alone cannot establish that the message taught them. The trials helped identify ambiguities and improve the design; they do not establish that an unknown intelligence would understand it. Read the trial account.

No set of 64 games is complete.

I chose games for their chess: brilliant attacks, surprising sacrifices, clever defenses, quiet strategy, and beautiful endings. The PGN anthology contains 64 games, while the binary message omits names, dates, and events.

There is a special joy in sharing something you love.

What could we share with a civilization that knows nothing about us? They might already know our science or lack the context for our art, but chess can be taught from scratch, revealing centuries of human imagination, mistakes, and brilliance.

Most likely, no one will ever receive this message. But even a small chance that someone might discover a position with a move like Bf5 makes the whole thing worth trying.

Industry observers note that yes. The chess-agnostic bootstrap, binary format and Python tools offer a starting point for teaching other subjects without a shared language or culture. Developers can adapt the system; researchers can use the trials to investigate what works, what fails and why. Source code and documentation.

In the source drawings, each cell reveals a bit: black represents 1 and white represents 0. Decoded pictures are reconstructed from the stored data, rather than cropped from the source square.

Industry observers note that colors, fine gray guides, and labels are added here to make the pictures easier to read. They are not part of the original message.

The intended recipient can infer these arrangements without visual aids, using bounding boxes, fixed sequence lengths, and other previously learned patterns.

Sources indicate that the frame below provides an example; its contents are explained later. The blue area covers a data row and its small marks underneath. The orange area picks out the small number to its left. The green area covers a whole boxed list. The gray guides make individual bit positions easier to count.

Hover over a colored phrase to keep only its matching highlights. Hover over the picture to hide all visual aids.

Recent findings suggest that the recipient begins with a clean sequence of bits or a sampled square, and is assumed to be able to count, recognize patterns and write simple programs. Obtaining those cells from a signal or physical object is a separate problem.

Sources indicate that the first task is to recover pictures and interactions from the bits. The recipient can then use those displays to learn chess. The bootstrap establishes the reading rules through worked examples; the recipient supplies a program that follows those rules. The message carries data for that program to interpret, not executable code.

The bootstrap is the narrow strip at the top of the view below. The payload area beneath it includes the unused space at the end.

Before looking inside each drawing, use its header to locate it in the strip. Each frame repeats the same corner mark. Its top row pairs a count of filled cells with a binary numeral to give its global number, 1–32. A second pair two rows below counts steps within a related group. That local count restarts for each group; standalone frames leave its row empty.

Compare these four headers. Frame 6 is sixth overall and second in its related group. Frame 3 stands alone:.

Frame 1: global 1 (00000001), group step 1 (00000001).

Frame 2: global 2 (00000010), group step 2 (00000010).

Frame 3: global 3 (00000011), no local counter.

Frame 6: global 6 (00000110), group step 2 (00000010).

The corner crop below demonstrates the same received pattern at four rotations:.

The repeated corner suggests an orientation to try. Ascending counts, dimensions and checksums test whether it remains consistent. The corner alone does not prove orientation or which received state should represent 1.

According to recent reports, binary numerals connect a pattern of bits to a quantity. This first frame makes that connection by pairing numbers with cells that can be counted.

The left-hand stripes contain 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 15 filled cells. Opposite each stripe, the upper four-bit numerals give the same quantity: the empty stripe pairs with 0000, and two filled cells pair with 0010. The lower eight-bit numerals repeat the quantities with leading zeros.

Recent findings suggest that A filled bit contributes a different amount depending on its position. Moving it one place left doubles that contribution. This frame pairs each single-bit pattern with its position number.

In a recent development, the left column starts with 00000001 and moves its single filled position one place left on each row, ending with 10000000. The right column counts those positions from 1 to 8, starting at the rightmost bit. Each horizontal pair belongs together.

Recent findings suggest that every field has a black border with a white inset around its data row. The border fixes the full width even when most positions are empty. The eight-bit patterns therefore stay in one column, while their four-bit position numbers stay in another.

A picture includes its empty positions as well as its filled ones. Its dimensions preserve the rectangle when the bits are inverted.

Sources indicate that the left picture has three rows and five columns. In its first row, the first position is empty and the second position is filled.

Sources indicate that the right picture keeps those same fifteen positions but exchanges filled and empty. The two numerals below the left picture are 3 and 5: row count, then column count. Both numerals end at the picture’s right edge. They count picture positions, not the source cells used to draw the blocks.

According to recent reports, without a shared reading order, the same sequence of values could produce different pictures. The numbered arrangement makes the order explicit.

The upper arrangement has 1, 2, 3 on its first row and 4, 5, 6 on its second. The lower sequence repeats 1 through 6. Finish each row from left to right before continuing on the next: this is row-major order.

A byte is a group of eight bits in a fixed order. This frame connects one compact group to its eight individual bit positions, establishing the unit used by later lengths and checks.

According to recent reports, the upper compact pattern is 00110101. The arrow below it leads to eight separate boxes containing the same bits in the same order. Read the single centre cell in each box: the first is empty, while the third is filled.

According to recent reports, the two numerals beneath that row are 00000001 and 00001000: one row, eight bit positions. The compact group above is one byte; the expanded row demonstrates its eight bits. Together, they establish one byte = eight bits. The lower half repeats this correspondence for 00001011.

A number spanning several bytes needs a byte order. Exchanging its high and low bytes can change its value, even though each byte still contains the same bits.

It has been revealed that each row repeats a sixteen-bit number at the left as its first eight bits in the middle and last eight bits at the right. Each has its own boundary, so an entirely zero high or low byte remains visible as a field. On the fifth row, 0001001000110100 splits into 00010010 and 00110100: decimal 18 and 52.

The first byte counts groups of 256; the second counts the remaining units. That row means 18×256 + 52 = 4,660. The next row reverses the bytes and represents 52×256 + 18 = 13,330. This is high-byte-first order. The notation u16 means a two-byte nonnegative integer; u32 means a four-byte one.

In a recent development, the recipient needs to locate the payload and know how much of the remaining square to read. These four measurements separate the bootstrap, used data and unused reserve.

In a recent development, top to bottom, the fields give the square side, 2,048; the first payload row, 64, counting from 0; the byte width, 8 bits; and the used payload length, 506,509 bytes. The first three fields have sixteen bits each; the last has thirty-two. Their right edges align, so the wider last field extends farther left.

Starting at row 64, read left to right across each row, then continue on the next. Each group of eight cells gives one byte, with its highest-value bit first. Recover exactly the declared number of bytes. Frame 32 demonstrates how the used length relates to the remaining capacity.

The recipient needs more than plausible-looking numbers before trusting the recovered lessons and games. A wrong orientation, bit interpretation or byte grouping can still produce values. Golden Board includes checks that let the recipient reject an inconsistent reading before using its content.

The content is organized into documents: collections of picture definitions, numerical data and display or interaction instructions. Each document’s bytes sit inside a checked block called a section. Its header identifies the document and gives its byte length. That length locates both the check at the end and the beginning of the next section.

Recent findings suggest that A section also stores a checksum, a value calculated from its identifying fields and content. The program creating the message computes this value from the original bytes. The recipient repeats the calculation on the recovered bytes and compares the result with the stored check. A mismatch rejects that reading. A match supports the consistency of those bytes; it does not repair them or establish that their meaning has been understood.

In a recent development, take section 2 from the actual payload. Its first six bytes form a header: the document’s number, called its ID, and the document’s byte length. The document itself follows, then the stored checksum. The calculation covers the header and every document byte, and stops before the stored check.

First eight bytes: 214 57 0 64 0 151 1 68.

Input to the calculation: header + complete document = 93,023 bytes.

Outside the calculation’s input.

Calculated from all 93,023 input bytes: 182 147 233 40.The four stored bytes match.

According to recent reports, golden Board uses CRC-32C for this calculation. The next drawings teach it with one input byte before applying the same method to a complete section. The immediate goal is to reproduce the sender’s check from the same bits.

Industry observers note that the checksum needs a way to combine bits and a way to test agreement. This frame defines both operations using every possible pair of inputs.

It has been revealed that the left-hand input columns list 00, 01, 10 and 11. Their results are 0, 1, 1, 0: XOR produces 1 when the inputs differ. The right-hand input columns repeat those pairs; their results are 1, 0, 0, 1: equality produces 1 when they agree.

Industry observers note that A right shift moves each bit one position to the right. This frame separates the shifted row from the bit that leaves its right edge; the checksum calculation uses both results.

According to recent reports, in the upper example, the input field ends in 00110101. The shifted field beneath it ends in 00011010. A zero enters at the far left, and the separate outgoing-bit box contains the 1 that left the input’s right edge.

The other examples repeat this layout with different input patterns. In the lowest example, the input ends in 0, and the outgoing-bit box has an empty centre. Its border preserves the result’s position even when the result is zero.

According to recent reports, both sender and recipient need the same constants to obtain the same checksum. The following calculations use the patterns shown here.

Sources indicate that the top field contains thirty-two ones. The middle field contains another thirty-two-bit pattern. The bottom field repeats that entire middle pattern and adds one leading 1. The fields line up at their right edges, making the added bit visible at the left.

Recent findings suggest that the lower fields are two forms of CRC-32C’s polynomial, the fixed pattern that identifies this CRC. The bottom form includes its leading bit. Keep the middle pattern for comparison with the changes between the states in Frame 12.

The checksum keeps a changing 32-bit working pattern, called its state. Combining an input byte with that pattern lets the byte affect the eventual check. This frame highlights the starting state, the first byte and the result of combining them.

Industry observers note that A shared outer box groups the two inputs: the all-ones state above and the input byte below. The state has four eight-bit bands. The input is 00110101, the pattern expanded in Frame 5, aligned under the rightmost band.

It has been revealed that applying Frame 8’s XOR rule to those eight aligned positions gives 11001010. The other three state bands have no input bits to change and remain all ones. The downward arrow leads from the grouped inputs to this four-band result. That result starts the eight bit rounds shown next.

In a recent development, the recipient must be able to calculate the next checksum state from the current one. This frame supplies a complete worked sequence, so the rule can be checked against every transition.

According to recent reports, the numbers at the right label the working patterns, from state 0 to state 9. The first row is the starting pattern; the second row is the byte-XOR result from Frame 11. Its last bit is 0. Shifting that row right gives exactly state 2.

It has been revealed that state 2’s rightmost bit is 1. Shift the entire pattern right. The top teal row in the comparison below is that calculated shift result. The bootstrap also supplies the next result, state 3, shown in the middle rose row. Comparing them reveals the extra change made in this round.

According to recent reports, line up matching positions in those two rows. In the cyan columns, the bits differ: the shift result has to be flipped to produce the supplied result. Put 1 at each differing position and 0 at every matching position. This is the XOR comparison learned in Frame 8. Its bottom row is the fixed feedback pattern: a map of which positions to flip.

We used the frame’s supplied result to identify that pattern. To calculate the round forward, shift state 2, then XOR the shift result with the feedback pattern. Those flips produce state 3. The outgoing 1 selects this feedback step, so the bit continues to affect the checksum after leaving the right edge.

The six remaining rounds use the same rule. Inspect the rightmost bit before shifting: an outgoing 0 needs only the shift; an outgoing 1 also needs the fixed XOR pattern. There are eight rounds after the byte-XOR step, ending at state 9. The table transcribes every supplied state and names the operation that produces it.

Sources indicate that the fixed XOR pattern exposed by Frame 12’s transitions is the middle pattern of Frame 10 read in reverse bit order. This relates the right-shift calculation to the polynomial shown there. It changes the interpretation of that constant; the bytes themselves keep the high-byte-first order established by Frame 6.

The last running state becomes a stored checksum through one final XOR. The recipient must distinguish that final value from the intermediate states used during calculation.

This repeats Frame 11’s grouped-input layout. XOR the state after eight rounds with the all-ones state above it. The arrow leads to the result, whose four bands read 87 | 111 | 14 | 252.

A second arrow leads to four separately bounded bytes. Each sits directly below the corresponding band of the result, with the same eight bits. Reading left to right preserves high-byte-first order. This is the check for the single input byte 00110101; the next frame compares a computed check with a stored one.

Industry observers note that A checksum becomes an integrity check by comparing the calculated value with a stored one. These three cases show the same equality test succeeding, failing, then succeeding again.

In the top case, the input field contains 00110101, read as 53. The computed check on the upper line and the stored check below it agree. The one-bit equality field at the right therefore contains 1, using the same boxed-bit convention as Frame 8.

The middle case changes the input to 00110100 but retains the check for the earlier pattern. The checks differ, so the equality field contains 0. The bottom case uses 00001011 with its own check and returns 1. These are checks of byte patterns, not of the characters used to print their decimal readings.

In a recent development, the recipient can now read numbers and reproduce a checksum. The next task is to find each section’s boundaries and recover the document inside it. The section is the checked storage wrapper; the document is the collection of things to display and use.

Those things are stored as records. Each record has a kind, a numeric name called an ID, and its own contents. For example, one record can define a small picture and another can refer to that picture by ID. Keeping the definition in one place lets many displays reuse it. IDs are assigned during message creation and stored in the data; the recipient reads them rather than inferring them from a shape. Their scope is one document.

It has been revealed that an inventory lists the documents that must be recovered and the records where each may be opened. These starting records are its entries. They lead to a picture sequence or an interaction. An entry is a record’s ID, not its byte address.

To teach these relationships, the bootstrap contains a complete small worked document of 326 bytes. Its simple pictures and responses exercise the format before chess appears. The next drawings describe that example, which is carried inside the strip. The full five-document payload below the strip uses the same rules.

Recent findings suggest that this frame divides a section into byte ranges. Its header declares how much body data follows, so the recipient can find the check and the next section.

Every row has three columns: start address, byte length, and the first address after the range. The ID row reads 0, 2, 2; the body-length-field row reads 2, 4, 6. Those two fields form the six-byte header. The body row reads 6, 326, 332, followed by the check row: 332, 4, 336.

Recent findings suggest that the section is therefore 336 bytes: six header bytes, 326 body bytes and four check bytes. These triples describe the layout; they are not extra fields stored in the header. The body-length value counts the body alone. The ID names the section; its meaning is established by the inventory example below.

Sources indicate that byte addresses must lead back to positions in the square. This frame connects each address to a physical row and column.

According to recent reports, the top line of each box gives a byte offset from the payload’s start and a bit index within that byte. Directly beneath them are the square row and square column. These are addresses for reading stored bits, so they start at zero; bit 0 is the first, leftmost bit of a byte. The labels in Frame 2 instead count binary places from the right, starting at one.

Sources indicate that each physical row holds 2,048 ÷ 8 = 256 bytes. The first group of 256 bytes therefore fills row 64: byte 0 starts at column 0, byte 1 at column 8, and byte 255 ends at column 2,047. Byte 256 starts the next row, 65, at column 0. These boundary cases appear in the third, fourth and fifth boxes.

According to recent reports, to locate another byte, count complete groups of 256 to find how many rows to move down from row 64. Within the remaining group, move eight columns for each byte, then add its bit index. This is why section boundaries need not coincide with physical row boundaries.

Dimensions preserve a picture’s complete rectangle, including white positions and entirely empty rows.

It has been revealed that for the upper-left matrix, the first numeral above it is 00000010: two rows of height. The next numeral is 00001000: eight columns of width. The other boxes use this same order, giving three rows by five columns, one by seven, and two by eight.

It has been revealed that the second row in the lower-right matrix is completely empty. Its eight positions still belong to the picture. Neither the empty row nor the white columns can be removed by cropping to the visible black shape.

According to recent reports, an object can be given a numeric name, then referred to by repeating that name. This frame separates names, reference counts and reference lists, with every target introduced before its use.

According to recent reports, each row has three parts: an eight-bit name on the left, an eight-bit reference count in the middle, and a boxed list on the right. The name does not specify the object’s size or its physical address.

The top row begins 00000110, read as 6. That pattern names the first object. Its count is 00000000, so the reference list is empty. The second row gives another name, 00000111 or 7, also with no references.

The third row begins 00001000, read as 8. Its count 00000001 claims one reference follows: 00000110, repeating the first row’s name.

Recent findings suggest that the bottom row begins 00001001, read as 9. Its count 00000010 notes two references follow: 00000111 and 00001000. These reach the second and third objects. Following the third object’s own reference then reaches the first. Counts and list lengths progress together: zero, zero, one, two.

This frame gives the miniature section’s actual fields and the exact range covered by its checksum. It places the stored check after that range, outside its own calculation.

Sources indicate that the three four-bit numerals on the left give the byte counts of the bands beside them: 0010, 0100, 0100 mean two, four and four bytes. The small marks under the data identify the start of each byte. These black numerals and marks belong to the original drawing. They describe how to read its bands; they do not add bytes to the section.

The first two data bands give section ID 1 and body length 326. The third band contains the four stored checksum bytes, 255 64 93 120.

The upper bounded range reads 0 | 332 | 332: start at byte zero, check 332 bytes, stop before address 332. The result below the arrow repeats the stored check’s bits. The lower bounded range is 332 | 4 | 336, locating those four check bytes after the covered range.

The covered range contains six header bytes and 326 body bytes. Start with the all-ones state, XOR the first byte into its low eight bits, and perform eight rounds. XOR the next byte into the resulting state and perform another eight rounds. Continue through every covered byte, then apply the final all-ones XOR once. Restart this process for each section. Calculating a separate finished checksum for every byte would lose the running state that joins the sequence. Frame 29 supplies all the bytes of this worked section.

The inventory lists the document sections required for a complete message. Here it contains one document: the worked miniature.

The six-byte header declares section ID 0 and body length 18. The next eighteen bytes are the inventory body, followed by its four checksum bytes, 113 28 238 100. Together they occupy 28 bytes: three full eight-byte rows and half of a fourth, starting at local row 31.

The first row contains the header and the beginning of the body. Row breaks are presentation boundaries, not section delimiters. ID 0 identifies the inventory; positive IDs identify documents. This small inventory lists only the worked document inside the bootstrap.

Sources indicate that the inventory identifies a document to recover and the records where reading it may begin. This frame expands the inventory body from Frame 20 into individual fields.

Sources indicate that the four-bit byte counts on the left use the convention from Frame 19. For example, 0010 beside the first band says that its value occupies two bytes. The value in that band is 1: one document.

In a recent development, the first three data bands give document count 1, document section ID 1 and document length 326. The next band contains 255 64 93 120, the expected checksum bytes for that document’s section. They match the check in Frame 19.

The entry count is 2. It gives the length of the boxed list of entry IDs 512 and 257. Each entry ID occupies two bytes, as its own left-hand count confirms. These IDs name records, rather than byte addresses; the next frames define those records.

According to recent reports, finding a document’s bytes does not yet tell the recipient how to draw its pictures or conduct its exercises. Its records divide that work into five kinds, all using the same named-record format.

It has been revealed that A glyph stores a small rectangular bitmap. A display frame places glyph IDs in a larger grid, so the same bitmap can be reused in many cells. A frame cell selects an entire glyph; it is distinct from either a source-message cell or one pixel inside the glyph. “Frame N of 32” continues to mean a bootstrap drawing; a numbered display-frame record belongs to a document.

It has been revealed that A trace starts from a frame and applies stored changes to indexed cells. This lets the message show a changing diagram or replay a game without storing every complete picture separately. A page combines a display with choices, accepted responses, feedback destinations and links. A table stores numbers alongside a trace; the lessons teach what those numbers mean.

Sources indicate that the worked document has 15 records: three glyphs, four display frames, one trace, one table and six pages. Its header names page 512 and trace 257 as entries. Each record begins with its kind, ID and content length; the record’s own contents are also called its payload. That length excludes the record’s seven-byte header. Read all the records before resolving their references: a target can occur later in the document.

Industry observers note that the player is the recipient’s program for interpreting these records and carrying out their display and interaction operations. A frame fixes which bitmap belongs in each cell. This guide displays equally sized tiles with enlarged glyphs inside them; tile size and spacing are presentation choices. The encoded dimensions count frame cells and glyph pixels.

It has been revealed that A document provides starting records and reusable bitmaps. This frame first defines its header, then two glyph records.

The top five data bands contain marker bytes 214, 57, entry count 2, record count 15, and entry IDs 512 and 257. The small rulers down the left count bytes. The markers below each band identify byte starts. Both are original black marks that describe the bands; neither contributes bytes to the serialized document. The table’s Bytes column transcribes the left-hand widths.

According to recent reports, the middle group and empty rectangle define glyph 0; the bottom group and patterned rectangle define glyph 1. Each record begins with kind 1, a two-byte ID and a four-byte payload length. Its three payload bytes give two rows, three columns and a packed bitmap.

It has been revealed that glyph 0 has bitmap byte 00000000, read as 0. Glyph 1 has 11010100, read as 212. Its first six bits form 110 / 101; two zero padding bits complete the byte. Both rectangles retain all three columns, including white pixels.

According to recent reports, the four-bit width ruler, 0010, counts two bytes. The data, 11010110 00111001, are the document marker bytes, read as 214 and 57. Marks below the data identify the start of each byte.

The document begins with these ten bytes, shown in decimal and grouped by field. Two-byte integers are stored high byte first.

It has been revealed that the band map identifies the fields in this sequence. Each entry ID takes two bytes: 2 0 is 512, and 1 1 is 257.

Glyph record 1 occupies miniature bytes 20–29: 1 0 1 0 0 0 3 2 3 212. Its seven-byte header gives kind, ID and payload length. Its three payload bytes give two rows, three columns and mask 212, or 11010100. The first six bits form 110 / 101; two zero padding bits complete the byte.

Glyph 0 is a separate record with an all-zero mask. Both glyphs retain their full two-row, three-column dimensions. Their IDs are names that display frames use to select these shapes. A frame cell containing 1 therefore selects glyph 1; it does not turn the whole cell into a single filled block.

Industry observers note that A display frame builds a larger picture by placing reusable glyphs at indexed positions. It can also assign names to positions that a later exercise lets the recipient select.

The record header identifies kind 2, ID 256 and payload length 18. The two dimension fields specify two rows and three columns. The six glyph IDs are 0,1,1 / 1,0,1, read across each row. Looking up those IDs produces the picture at the lower left. The left-hand rulers give each band’s byte width.

It has been revealed that glyph IDs fit in one byte, so these six frame cells occupy six bytes. Record headers still use two-byte IDs. The width of a reference depends on the field that carries it.

After those cells, a count of 2 introduces two selection definitions. Each definition contains a region ID followed by a cell index. The first definition is 10 | 0: region 10 selects cell 0, the upper-left position. The second definition is 20 | 5: region 20 selects cell 5, the lower-right position. The matching highlights connect each pair to its picture position and its index box.

The resulting picture and the indices of its six cells:.

A trace changes an initial frame through ordered partial updates. A cell keeps its previous glyph until an revision names that cell.

Industry observers note that the prefix bands identify kind 3, trace 257, payload length 19, initial frame 256, one attached table 400 and two patch steps. The rulers on the left count bytes. The upper picture is the referenced initial frame.

According to recent reports, the first patch group and changed cell in the middle picture contain three fields: assignment count 1, cell index 0, glyph ID 1. Apply that assignment to the initial picture: its upper-left cell now shows glyph 1, while the other five cells keep their values.

Industry observers note that the second patch group and changed cell in the bottom picture also have one assignment: cell 5 receives glyph 0. Apply it to the middle state, not to a fresh copy of the initial frame. The result is 1,1,1 / 1,0,0. Two patches therefore produce three pictures, and the first patch’s change survives the second.

Each assignment replaces the cell’s glyph ID. Assigning 0 selects the blank glyph; leaving a cell out of the patch preserves its current value. The changes affect this trace’s display state, so the reusable initial-frame record remains available as the starting point.

This frame defines an exercise page that connects a picture, a response and its outcomes. A display alone cannot say what the recipient should select or what follows a submission.

Sources indicate that the first three bands identify kind 4 page 512 and its 26-byte payload. The next pair selects frame 256: display flag 0 identifies the displayed frame. The page’s kind and its display flag are separate fields.

According to recent reports, the response fields request a set of selected region IDs and offer 10 and 20. The acceptance fields declare one accepted set of length one: [10]. The bottom fields name success page 514, failure page 515, demonstration page 516 and one explicit link to 516. The rulers beside the bands count bytes; list counts and list contents remain separate fields.

Page 512 uses the region mappings taught in Frame 23: region 10 identifies cell 0, and region 20 identifies cell 5. A selection records a region ID; it does not replace the glyph displayed in that cell. Page 512 treats its response as a set of distinct IDs, so their selection order does not affect acceptance. Selecting a region again removes it from the set. The complete submitted set must match a stored accepted response: choosing both 10 and 20 fails, even though it includes the accepted choice 10.

A page can also display a trace: display flag 1 selects that form, while 0 selects a fixed frame. The demonstration page in the complete graph below uses a trace. The response shape is independent of this display choice. Shape 1 keeps one selection, replacing it when another is chosen; shape 2 keeps a set; shape 3 appends an ordered sequence, preserving repeats. A sequence is bounded by the number of choices exposed on that page.

Sources indicate that shape 0 is a passive page: it has a display and links but no response to submit. Its fields for success, failure and passive pages contain the reserved value 65,535, meaning no reference. This value never names a record. Glyph 0, by comparison, is a real record and can be drawn.

This frame connects each submitted choice to the feedback page and picture it opens. It first defines the contrasting glyph used by the failure picture.

Industry observers note that the upper bands and small rectangle define glyph 2: two rows, three columns, bitmap byte 00101000. Its first six bits form 001 / 010; the last two are padding. The white first column remains part of the glyph.

It has been revealed that the four-bit numerals beside the upper bands give their byte widths: 1, 2, 4, 1, 1, 1. Width and value are different: the 0100 beside the payload-length field indicates that the value 3 is written in four bytes. The longer patterns at the lower left are submitted region IDs, not width labels.

Industry observers note that the submitted ID 10 leads to page 514 and frame 259, filled with glyph 1. The submitted ID 20 leads to page 515 and frame 260, filled with glyph 2. Each feedback box gives page kind and ID, then display flag and frame ID, then the resulting picture.

Selecting a region edits a pending answer; committing evaluates it. These three cases show the difference.

Sources indicate that the top case uses operation 1 with argument 10 to select region 10. The line below shows that page 512 stays active. The middle case uses operation 3 with argument 0 to clear the pending selection; the page again stays 512.

According to recent reports, the bottom case and its feedback picture use operation 2 with argument 0 to commit that now-empty set. It is not the accepted set [10], so the result is page 515, displaying glyph 2 in every cell. These are examples of actions, not additional serialized packets.

Commit records the pending answer, compares it with the page’s accepted responses, and opens the stored success or failure page with an empty selection. Doing nothing submits no answer; committing an empty selection submits an answer of length zero. Later lessons use this distinction when an empty answer is correct.

Stored page references determine what opens next. Their numeric order does not define a sequence of pages.

Sources indicate that the first pair maps submitted region 20 to failure page 515. The second pair and upper picture map region 10 to success page 514. The third pair and lower picture have a different role: demonstration page 516 links to final-picture page 518.

Page 516 plays trace 257 and also links to feedback page 517. Completing its two patches does not follow either link automatically. Pages 514, 515, 517 and 518 each link back to question 512.

Following a return link starts a fresh attempt with an empty selection. Reset only clears a pending answer on a question page; it cannot erase a submitted answer from a feedback page. The explicit links also let a learner open the demonstration without first answering correctly.

This frame supplies the complete miniature document inside its checked section. It lets the recipient test the earlier boundaries and record examples together.

The first six bytes are header bytes 0 1 | 0 0 1 70: ID 1 and body length 326. The 326-byte body begins with 214 57 | 0 2 | 0 15 | 2 0 | 1 1 and contains all fifteen records. The last four bytes are 255 64 93 120. The total is 6+326+4 = 336 bytes, filling exactly forty-two eight-byte rows starting at local row 12.

The final row contains four body bytes and four check bytes. There is no partial data row. The reader can verify this section’s check now; parsing every record also requires the table format shown next. This worked section belongs to the strip, not to the five-document payload below it.

Sources indicate that table values are unsigned numbers. A value here does not select a glyph, as a frame cell does.

It has been revealed that the first three bands specify kind 5, ID 400 and payload length 17. The dimension fields give two rows and three columns. The last two bands contain 0,1,2 and 3,4,5, each value stored as a u16. Thus each value band occupies six bytes.

It has been revealed that the four-bit widths on the left count the bytes in each band. The two value bands each have width 0110, or six bytes: three values with two bytes each. Their small under-row marks locate those byte boundaries.

Trace 257 refers to this table as attached data. The record reader recovers its values without assigning them a subject-specific meaning. Later tables use the same format for move words, scores and field widths; the displayed lessons teach those meanings.

A trace’s references make its attached tables available to the reader. Its stored patches give the display changes explicitly; the player does not calculate those changes from the table values.

The final two bootstrap frames show how sections form a stream and where the full message’s used data ends. Together with the earlier examples, the strip defines the byte order, checksum, section and inventory layouts, document header, and five record types needed to read the payload.

In a recent development, this frame places sections consecutively and distinguishes the final byte from the address after it. The recipient needs both to stop at the correct boundary.

The upper rows have four columns: section ID, start, exclusive end and length. The inventory row is 0,0,28,28; the document row is 1,28,364,336. The second section begins exactly where the first ends. These rows describe placement, not extra header fields.

Industry observers note that the 0,1,2 line is a counting sequence; this example contains only sections 0 and 1. The bottom pair contrasts last included byte 363 with exclusive end 364. In general, the next section starts after six header bytes, the declared body length and four check bytes.

It has been revealed that this frame separates the full payload’s used bytes from its zero-filled reserve. The recipient must stop parsing at the used end and check what remains.

The four bounded fields give start offset 0, used length 506,509, capacity 507,904, and reserve length 1,395. The small tallies at the right number these rows.

Sources indicate that the lower example contains two separately bounded fields: thirty-two zero bits above, and the eight-bit numeral 00100000 below, read as 32. The first field is data; the second states its width. Their separate boundaries keep the numeral’s filled bit out of the zero data.

It has been revealed that the five document bodies total 506,181 bytes. Add 268 inventory-body bytes and 60 bytes of section headers and checks to obtain 506,509 used bytes. The remaining 1,395 bytes must be zero rather than another document.

It has been revealed that the reader starts at row 64 and uses Frame 16’s mapping to recover the declared number of bytes. For each section, it reads the header, checks that the body fits within the remaining data, verifies the checksum, and advances past header, body and check. Section IDs increase from 0, and each required document appears once.

Section 0 is the full message’s inventory. Its body begins with the two-byte document count 5. Each document entry specifies an ID, body length, section checksum, entry count and ordered entry IDs. The inventory contains these numeric declarations, not lesson titles or a curriculum order.

In a recent development, A complete reading must match the inventory to the received sections and document headers. It must also validate record lengths, kinds, references and cell indices. Missing objects and invalid references cause rejection; the reader does not guess replacements. Successfully displaying one fragment is not enough to accept the whole message.

The supplied Python decoder implements these rules directly. It tests rotations, reflections and swapped bit states, compares the bootstrap with its defined drawings, and requires one completely valid reading. This is a check of a known format. Discovering that format from the drawings is the recipient’s separate task.

In a recent development, the miniature belongs to the bootstrap strip. It demonstrates the format used by the inventory and five complete documents in the byte stream below it. After recovering and validating that full set, the recipient can open a declared entry.

It has been revealed that the player can now look up the entry’s records and display them. No chess knowledge is needed to reconstruct the picture in the next example.

Follow document 2, which stores the complete games, and its first declared entry, trace 324. We will reconstruct its initial picture using the bootstrap’s rules, then use the course to interpret that picture as chess.

According to recent reports, after all six sections have been recovered and checked, the inventory identifies document 2 with a body of 93,017 bytes. Its section starts at payload byte 13,533. The six-byte header reads 0 2 | 0 1 107 89: document ID, then body length, high byte first. The body begins six bytes later, at payload byte 13,539. Document offset 0 means this point.

Industry observers note that the first eight body bytes come from source row 116, columns 1,816–1,879. They are one continuous row of 64 cells in the message; the illustration regroups them into eight rows, one byte per row. The first two bytes identify the document format. The next two declare 64 entries; the following two declare 151 records. The last pair shown is the first entry ID.

Recent findings suggest that entry 324 is a stored name, not the location of the next byte. The remaining 63 entry IDs follow it. All 64 entries occupy 128 bytes after the six-byte header, so the records begin at document byte 6 + 64×2 = 134.

At each record, read its one-byte kind, two-byte ID and four-byte content length. Consume exactly that many content bytes, then continue with the next record. For example, record 0 starts at byte 134 and declares three content bytes. Its seven-byte header and three-byte contents end at byte 144, where the next record starts. Reading all 151 records builds a lookup from each ID to its stored contents.

Looking up the declared entry 324 finds a trace, kind 3. Its first two content bytes are 00000001 00000000, or 1×256 + 0 = 256: its initial display-frame ID. Looking up 256 finds the frame record above. This follows a reference back to an earlier record; it does not jump to byte 256. The rest of the trace contains its attached tables and ordered updates. Its initial display uses this frame before applying any revision.

Frame 256 begins its contents with 00001001 00001000: nine rows and eight columns. The next 9×8 = 72 bytes give one glyph ID for each frame cell, across each row and then down. Here are those actual bytes, shown as decimal IDs. The row and column labels are added for reading. After the grid, two zero bytes give a selectable-region count of 0. The frame’s contents therefore occupy 2 + 72 + 2 = 76 bytes, matching its header.

Cell 48 is row 6, column 0, because 6×8 + 0 = 48. Its byte is 00100000, or ID 32. The frame record starts at byte 355. After its seven-byte header and two dimension bytes, the grid begins at 355 + 7 + 2 = 364. Cell 48 is therefore at document byte 364 + 48 = 412, or payload byte 13,539 + 412 = 13,951. The mapping from Frame 16 places it at source row 118, columns 1,016–1,023. The byte names a glyph; its eight source bits do not themselves draw that glyph.

Sources indicate that record 32 is a glyph, kind 1. Its six content bytes are 5 5 | 1 8 64 0: row count, column count, then the packed bitmap. The dimensions require 5×5 = 25 picture bits. The four bitmap bytes carry those first 25 bits, followed by seven zero padding bits that complete the last byte. Take five picture bits at a time to fill each bitmap row from left to right, then continue on the next row. The padding completes the stored bytes and is excluded from the picture.

Industry observers note that the recipient now draws that bitmap in frame cell 48. Each of the other cells is drawn by looking up its own glyph ID in this same document. A repeated ID reuses the same bitmap. Record 0 has contents 2 2 | 0: a two-by-two bitmap of zero bits. It supplies the blank tiles wherever the frame names glyph 0. The result is the complete initial picture of entry 324:.

It has been revealed that every glyph shape now comes from a stored bitmap, and every position from a stored frame cell. The recipient can draw this picture using the bootstrap’s rules alone. Learning what the shapes, arrangement and bottom row mean is the next task for the recovered course. Later, we will return to this same trace and apply its first stored patch.

The picture just recovered is a display the recipient can draw before understanding chess. Document 1 supplies the visual vocabulary; the chess course then explains the 8×8 board, two sides, six piece types, starting positions and alternating turns. This guide uses the usual English names, White and Black; White moves first. The recipient has no reason to associate any particular shape with a chess piece, so the glyphs could be arbitrary. I chose patterns that resemble familiar chess pieces. Their roles still have to be taught through setup, movement and repeated examples.

Industry observers note that the study route begins with document 1’s representation lessons, then documents 3, 4 and 5: elementary rules, practical rules and history, then relationships and limited strategic guidance. Document 2 supplies the complete-game anthology.

A worked example demonstrates an input and its result. Contrasts make a distinction visible by showing a rejected result or changing a condition such as a blocker or a castling right. Practice asks the recipient to choose among stored alternatives, using the page mechanism from the bootstrap. A page can group several questions: the learner selects an answer for each and commits the combined set. The player checks that whole set against the page’s stored accepted responses.

Sources indicate that A passive route indicates the explanations and feedback without requiring a correct submission. Both routes use the same record operations. The chess calculations happen when the lessons are authored; the player later presents the resulting pictures, choices and feedback.

Sources indicate that A glyph ID remains a local name. Its role as a pawn, knight or other piece comes from the examples. The same glyph can appear on the board, identify a selected piece in a question, and appear at its destination after a move.

Recent findings suggest that A question must identify its subject as well as show a board. This knight lesson uses a 29×10 display frame containing an 8×8 board and a separate 8×8 answer grid, or mask, below it. A footer between them names the side, selected piece, square and question type.

Here the footer selects the first-side knight at board row 7, column 1, or b1 in the added chess coordinates. The question asks for legal destinations. The knight can move to a3 and c3. Its jump also reaches d2 geometrically, but a friendly pawn occupies that square.

Document 3, trace 3068, step 33. Within this 29×10 display frame, the board occupies rows 1–8 and columns 1–8; the mask occupies rows 11–18 and columns 1–8; the footer is row 9. Coordinates start at 0. The mask’s plus-shaped glyph 5 marks indices 40 and 42 within the 8×8 mask, corresponding to a3 and c3. This illustration highlights the stored answer.

Industry observers note that an ordinary capture removes the opposing piece at the destination and puts the moving piece there. A friendly piece prevents a move to that square. A legal move must also leave its own king safe. An attack on the king is check; check with no legal escape is checkmate. The king stays on the board when the game ends.

King safety depends on the resulting position. In one course example, a king on e1 tries to capture a bishop on d1 while an opposing rook stands on f1. Before the move, the king itself blocks the rook’s line to d1. Once the king leaves e1, that line opens, so the capture is illegal. The course shows the attempted move’s resulting occupancy and attack. Testing a king capture means moving the king, removing the captured piece, and checking its destination in that changed position.

Sources indicate that control follows a piece’s movement geometry in the displayed position. For a rook, bishop or queen, it extends along each permitted straight line to the first occupied square, including a friendly piece it defends. Pins do not remove controlled squares. Here the bishop on b5 points along a diagonal through the knight on c6 toward the knight’s king on e8. Moving the knight would expose the king. The knight still controls eight squares, but has no legal destination.

A side with no legal move is checkmated if its king is in check, and stalemated otherwise. Checkmate is a loss; stalemate is a draw. Golden Board also recognizes three classes where neither side can give checkmate: king against king, king and bishop against king, and king and knight against king. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flapping Airplanes wants to train AI with less data and get more out of each chip.

In a recent development, databricks has published a guide and open code for running five tabular foundation models, AI that makes predictions from spreadsheet-style data without task-specific training, on its AI Runtime GPU service. It indicates the models cost more per prediction than XGBoost on CPUs, and two need a commercial deal with their makers.

In a recent development, databricks has published a guide to running “tabular foundation models” on its platform, the company said in a blog post on Monday. These AI models make predictions from spreadsheet-style data without being trained for each task. The guide comes with free code that compares five of them.

Businesses use table data to predict things like credit risk, customer churn and demand. Usually, teams build and retrain a separate model for every task. Tabular foundation models are instead pretrained on millions of made-up datasets, then learn from a company’s example rows at the moment they predict.

The idea is catching on. SAP, which works closely with Databricks, closed a €1B-plus deal for Prior Labs, maker of the TabPFN model, in July. H2O.ai launched its own model in May.

Databricks is open about the trade-offs. Running these models on GPUs costs more per prediction than a classic XGBoost model on an ordinary processor, it claims. Memory use also grows with every row, because the model reads the whole training set each time.

Licences are another catch. Of the models Databricks lists, TabICLv2, Mitra v2 and KumoTabular can be used commercially. TabFM and the newest TabPFN need a separate deal with their makers.

In a recent development, the pitch is for Databricks’ AI Runtime, a pay-as-you-go GPU service in preview since March. Databricks indicates its Nvidia H100 chips can run TabPFN-3 on tables of up to 1 million rows and 200 columns. The company, recently valued at $190B, still advises firms to test the models on their own data first.

There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a newly introduced advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a substantial upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week, iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many newly introduced capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

It has been revealed that the one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole fresh set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:.

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

Recent findings suggest that I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m right now viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

Recent findings suggest that in theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch. For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

Have you tried Siri AI’s latest Notes features in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

Cognition and McKinsey team up to sell Devin, its AI coder, to massive firms

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cognition, the maker of the AI coding agent Devin, has formed an alliance with McKinsey & Company, the two firms declared on Monday.
  • According to recent reports, mcKinsey will help clients pick the engineering projects that matter most and set a baseline for cost, speed and quality.
  • “Together, we can help leaders put that added engineering capacity to work and connect it to measurable business outcomes and return on investment,” stated Russell Kaplan, Cognition’s co-founder and president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cognition, the maker of the AI coding agent Devin, has formed an alliance with McKinsey & Company, the two firms declared on Monday. They will sell AI software engineering to large companies in the US and Europe.

According to recent reports, mcKinsey will help clients pick the engineering projects that matter most and set a baseline for cost, speed and quality. It will also help them redesign teams and workflows around AI. Cognition will provide Devin, which takes on engineering work and brings it back for review.

“Together, we can help leaders put that added engineering capacity to work and connect it to measurable business outcomes and return on investment,” stated Russell Kaplan, Cognition’s co-founder and president.

The firms cite a McKinsey survey of 334 product and engineering leaders from the second quarter of 2026. In the top quarter of organisations, AI more than doubled productivity. At 30% of them, productivity fell.

Lari Hämäläinen is a senior partner in McKinsey’s technology, media and telecoms practice. He told Business Insider’s Tim Paradis that until late 2025, many AI coding tools were useful only for narrow tasks. More capable models now handle longer, more autonomous coding work, he stated.

“It’s a completely different thing to scale it across 2,000 developers or 20,000 developers,” he mentioned.

McKinsey indicates it has helped more than 50 companies redesign their software development around AI.

In a recent development, cognition says Devin works with several AI models and matches each one to a different kind of work. It says this gives companies frontier-level performance for 60% less. Art Levy, its vice president of global partnerships, told Business Insider that pricier models can go to the harder work.

“You don’t need to drive a Ferrari to the grocery store,” Levy said.

Cognition notes it works with six of the eight global systemically important banks. It also counts three of the six largest health insurers as clients. European software company Comarch is using Devin to rebuild its 20-year-old ERP XL system in 18 months. It is also working with McKinsey to bring that work to more teams.

Cognition brought in Alex Stamos as its security chief in September, after a funding round at $48bn. In October, Business Insider reported it was weighing newly introduced funding at up to $80bn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This holiday season, you're likely to see deals galore on a range of Fitbit models, including the popular Fitbit Air, Fitbit Edge, and Fitbit Charge 6,.

It has been revealed that these are easily three of the best fitness trackers you can buy. But how do you choose between them?

In a recent development, that's where I come in. Hi, I'm Dan, and I lead TG's wearable tech coverage. More importantly, I'm fresh off reviewing the Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Air, and have worn/tested the Fitbit Charge 6 extensively.

According to recent reports, I already covered the Fitbit Air vs. Fitbit Charge 6 and Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Charge 6, while my colleague Jane went in depth on the Fitbit Edge vs. Fitbit Air.

Recent findings suggest that now let's compare all three across six major categories, including cost, design, display, fitness tracking, health and safety features, and battery life. And at the end, I'll tell you which one I'd spend my hard-earned cash on.

In a recent development, the Fitbit Air is the most affordable of the three, with a starting price of just $99. Meanwhile, the Fitbit Charge 6 retails for $159, and the Fitbit Edge is $179. However, these prices don't tell the whole story.

While the Fitbit Edge and Air are upcoming for 2026, the Fitbit Charge 6 is from 2023. This means it's far more likely to see a hefty discount at any given time than its siblings, especially this holiday season. For example, Amazon has the Charge 6 for $122 right now, but I wouldn't be surprised to see it drop to $99 or less in the coming weeks.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Winner: Fitbit Air or Fitbit Charge 6 (if it's on sale).

The Fitbit Edge, Fitbit Air, and Fitbit Charge 6 are lightweight, comfortable devices with minimal footprints, making them appealing sleep trackers as well as fitness trackers (I loathe sleeping with chunky tech on my wrist).

The Fitbit Edge is the largest and heaviest of the bunch, but not by much. On the wrist, without looking, I'd be genuinely hard-pressed to tell the Fitbit Edge from the Fitbit Charge 6. The Air, meanwhile, truly lives up to its name.

With no display, buttons, or GPS, the Fitbit Air is by far the lightest and the most compact of the three. The low-key design also means it doesn't shout to the world, "I'm a fitness tracker, this guy cares about his health!" In fact, I can even rock it with a traditional mechanical watch on the other wrist without looking like a total dweeb.

The most discreet and comfortable of the bunch, the Fitbit Air's design is easily my favorite.

Industry observers note that the Fitbit Air doesn't have a display, so it obviously won't be winning this category, but the Fitbit Edge and Fitbit Charge 6 do. Both are touch-sensitive AMOLEDs, but the Edge's display is larger and brighter, making it easier to view in direct daylight.

Recent findings suggest that it's also more finger-friendly to interact with, especially if you have meaty paws. I have fairly standard fingers (I think?) and still find the Charge 6's 1.04-inch display to be a bit fiddly. This is not the case for the Edge's 1.34-inch panel.

All three wearables are competent fitness trackers capable of recording a wide range of common workout types accurately, but the Edge has some notable advantages over its peers.

For example, if your workout habits involve mountain activities or you simply like going for a jog/walk without carrying a smartphone, the Fitbit Edge is going to be your best option of the three.

If your workout habits involve mountain activities or you simply like going for a jog/walk without carrying a smartphone, the Fitbit Edge is your best option.

Sources indicate that this is because the Fitbit Air lacks onboard GPS for location tracking. Sure, it's still capable of reporting location-based metrics like distance and pace, but the Air relies on your paired smartphone's GPS antenna to make it happen. Translation: you have to lug around an extra chunk of tech.

The Fitbit Charge 6 has an onboard GPS antenna, so you can leave your phone at home, but it lacks a barometric altimeter for precise elevation tracking. If you live somewhere flat, this might not matter much.

In a recent development, however, I live in hilly Seattle, Washington, where an afternoon walk might involve 500+ feet of elevation gain. Fortunately, the newer Edge has both GPS and an altimeter, making it my top pick for fitness tracking.

The Fitbit Air, Fitbit Edge, and Fitbit Charge 6 all use the same Google Health app (formerly the Fitbit app), where owners can view their workout history, daily sleep reports, set wellness goals, view long-term trend data, and more.

All three models also support blood oxygen saturation readings (Sp02), but only the Edge and Charge 6 can perform ECGs.

Meanwhile, only the newer models (Edge and Air) offer Google's most advanced health and safety features, borrowed from the Pixel Watch 5 line. These include breathing emergency alerts and loss of pulse detection, as well as Google's upcoming monthly insulin resistance and blood pressure trend reports.

All three Fitbits are billed as lasting up to a week per charge, but in my experience, the older Fitbit Charge 6 falls short of that by a day or two. The Fitbit Edge, meanwhile, has no issue lasting a week on a single charge, but there's a catch.

When using the Edge's onboard GPS to log an outdoor workout, the battery drains rapidly: up to 12% per hour.

Industry observers note that with no GPS or screen to power, you might guess that the Fitbit Air has the best real-world battery life of the three. And you'd be right. The Fitbit Air should last you seven days per charge with no problem, regardless of how many workouts you log.

While I ultimately prefer the price and low-key, diminutive design of the Fitbit Air to the Fitbit Edge and Charge 6, the Edge has its peers beat when it comes to fitness tracking performance, screen size/quality, and health/safety features.

Sure, it's the priciest of the bunch, but the Fitbit Edge is definitely the model I'm most likely to spend my hard-earned cash on. Which Fitbit model would you choose? Let me know in the poll below.

In the past year alone, Dan has assessed major product releases from the likes of Apple, Garmin, Google, Samsung, Polar and many others.

An avid outdoor adventurer, Dan is based in the U.S. Pacific Northwest where he takes advantage of the beautiful surroundings every chance he gets. Today, Apple is adding UFC into the mix, so MMA fans can track the fights live through the unified Apple Sports experience.

Apple Sports will provide coverage of every bout across the full fight card, with live stats like total strike counts, takedowns, knockdowns and more.

Apple Sports features animated background artwork to differentiate different games and matches in the detail view, and UFC is no different with a custom backdrop that evokes the ambience of being under the lights of the Octagon. You can keep up with the action inside the app, or tap the clock icon to start a Live Activity and get score updates delivered directly to your iPhone’s lock screen.

Sources indicate that apple Sports now comes preinstalled when setting up a upcoming iPhone from scratch. If you don’t already have it, you can get it as a free download from the App Store.

The Sports app is still only available on iPhone right now though; Apple has still not announced aims to do an iPad and Mac native version. You can have the Sports Live Activities from your iPhone show up on Apple Watch and Mac, however.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the uncertainty in the Middle East and concerns about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom and high spending continue to weigh on investor sentiment. Investors can consider strengthening their portfolios by adding dividend stocks.

Tracking top Wall Street analysts can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts provide useful insights after thorough analysis of a company's financials and growth prospects.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

This week's first dividend pick is natural gas producer Expand Energy, which recently announced the $1.25 billion acquisition of Twin Eagle Holdings, a private asset-backed natural gas marketing and optimization business. The deal is expected to accelerate EXE's marketing and commercial goals.

Meanwhile, Expand Energy impressed investors with solid second-quarter results. It repurchased shares worth $530 million in Q2 2026 and unveiled an additional $1 billion of buyback authorization. Expand declared a dividend of nearly 58 cents per share, payable on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend per share of $2.30, EXE stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

It has been revealed that following the Q2 print, Wolfe Research analyst Doug Leggate reiterated a buy rating on EXE stock and raised his price target to $114 from $110. The five-star analyst noted that Expand delivered market-beating adjusted earnings per share and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, driven by better gas realizations and lower gathering, processing, and transportation expenses.

"Solid 2Q26 with in-line guidance keeps our focus on what it can control, walking the line between options to return value to s/holders," remarked Leggate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

But Mount played only 18 minutes of Saturday’s 1-1 draw against the European champions in Gothenburg before being replaced by Scotland international Tyler Fletcher.

“He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

“We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”.

Post-match video footage indicated Mount walking freely on to the United bus without the aid of a protective boot or knee support.

According to recent reports, michael Carrick told VG Mason Mount was taken off as a precaution. Looked OK leaving stadium. pic.twitter.com/Uo0fBtgpAl.

United went behind within two minutes at the Ullevi Stadium when Liverpool target Ibrahim Mbaye punished slack marking to put PSG ahead.

Bryan Mbeumo fired United level after 32 minutes following good work from Amad Diallo, the Cameroon forward’s third goal in two games after his match-winning double against Atletico Madrid.

United meet Leeds in a Dublin friendly on Wednesday before coming up against AC Milan and their former manager Ruben Amorim next Saturday.

United open their Premier League campaign at Hull on August 22.

It has been revealed that “It was good game. PSG is good so we had to keep building fitness. I am happy to have other [players] back and we have to keep going.”.

It has been revealed that “It’s good for me. I enjoyed it. We need to build fitness, we have a substantial season ahead.”.

“It’s a good game PSG are tough to beat and we got a draw and now think about the next game [against Leeds in Dublin].”.

It has been revealed that “We have two more games against Leeds a and Milan. We need to have major season and hope to win a trophy.”.

Recent findings suggest that all over in Gothenburg and it’s been a good match for Michael Carrick’s team. They looked sharper and quicker than their win over Atletico Madrid last week (what the manager wanted) and things are moving in the right direction. Two things to worry about, however, were the early exits of Mason Mount and Tom Heaton with injuries. They’ll especially hope the Mount knock isn’t anything mid or long term.

It has been revealed that nearly done and it’s been a good run out for United. They’ve looked the better, sharper side and, if anything, deserve to win. In mitigation, this is United fourth pre-season game to PSG’s second...

Industry observers note that fernandes has one thing on his mind when he gets the ball 25 yards out in the centre of the park - a shot. He unleashes the attempt, destined for the bottom-left corner, forcing Longoni, the sub goalkeeper, into a good save.

Tielemans’s first bit of brilliance from the Belgian there.

United on top in this half, as they were in the first.

“Get a bit sharper, get better on the ball, go up a notch.”.

Manchester United continue their Sweden sojourn with match against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.

Clearly a clash against the back-to-back Champions League winners is a step up from their previous two pre-season friendlies (victories against Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid), but at the same time this is more a chance for players to get miles in the legs and see how new signings and possibly some young guns fit in.

One of those upcoming signings is Youri Tielemans, and the Belgian international is in line to make his debut after his move from Aston Villa. Other team news is that Bruno Fernandes is back and ready to captain the team.

Michael Carrick has also been boosted by the returns of Matheus Cunha, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui after their post-World Cup breaks.

Cunha, however, will not play a part in today’s match because of a “minor illness” according to the MUTV website. He is expected to link up with the squad in Ireland, where they face Leeds United at Croke Park, after the match.

This will be Man Utd’s first outing since the 2-1 win over Atletico, a performance and result that pleased Carrick.

“I enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot of good in things that we are looking to improve on,” the United manager stated. “Building on what we did for the last seven months, I think there is a lot of good signs for us, it’s never going to be the exact stage we want to be at. But I thought there was really a lot of positives to take out of the game, individual, collectively as a team, senior players looking strong and fit, and the younger players doing really well.

“The spirit and the camaraderie is so vital for the team, it’s great to see the boys getting on so naturally and enjoying each other’s company. Collectively we looked strong as a team, which is always the most important thing, and individual performances seeing the young players come on to have an impact.”.

Kick-off is set for 4pm so stay here for the build up, team news and action.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after this week’s Carbon availability, Google today unveiled Gemini 4 Hydrogen instead of keeping the “Flash” branding. This model is billed as bringing “cutting-edge intelligence to everyone.”.

Recent findings suggest that compared to Gemini 3.8 Flash (which launched in September), Hydrogen is billed as a “major standalone upgrade” with “significant leaps in both speed and intelligence.” It offers native 1 million-token input and up to 1 million output tokens. Specifically:.

“Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class.”.

In the Gemini app, Hydrogen is better at following and sticking to your tone, format, and rules, while offering clear tables and visual breakdowns. As such, “email drafts, study guides, rewrites, and documents come back ready to use on the first try.” Additionally, Hydrogen “more frequently calls the right tools (i.e., Connected Apps) and skills for the job.”.

In the model picker, 4 Hydrogen is billed as providing “Everyday help.”.

Free users in the Gemini app get access to Hydrogen via the “[Auto] model selection when it’s the appropriate model for the prompt.”.

Google claims Hydrogen significantly upgrades Search (AI Mode) by better understanding your intent:.

…you can ask your question in your natural flow of thought — even if you have multiple parts to your query, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests — and Search will intelligently comprehend what you’re looking for.

Industry observers note that responses get more visual and will feature a wider range of relevant links. Hydrogen is the default model for AI Mode and is used for “your hardest questions” in AI Overviews.

This was a nice surprise when I opened the app an hour or two ago. It seems to be noticeably better, too.

In Google Antigravity, 4 Hydrogen has an “Extra” thinking tier alongside Low, Medium, and High. Then there’s Orchestrator: “Carbon that may offload routine steps to Hydrogen. Same Carbon-level quality, fewer tokens used.”.

To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity. Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session.

For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs.

For developers, Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that langChain, which makes tools for building and running AI agents, has raised $300m at a $3bn valuation, the firm revealed on Friday.
  • It has been revealed that capitalG, Alphabet’s independent growth fund and an existing investor, led the round.
  • The valuation is more than double the $1.25bn of about a year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that langChain, which makes tools for building and running AI agents, has raised $300m at a $3bn valuation, the firm revealed on Friday. The Series C brings its total funding to $460m.

It has been revealed that capitalG, Alphabet’s independent growth fund and an existing investor, led the round. Newly introduced investors GIC and DFJ Growth and existing investors IVP and Sapphire Ventures also took part. Salesforce Ventures, Insight Venture Partners, QuantumLight and MongoDB Ventures joined as new investors. Sequoia, Amplify and Benchmark put in more.

The valuation is more than double the $1.25bn of about a year ago. LangChain then raised $125m in a round led by IVP, TechCrunch reported.

Industry observers note that langChain began in 2022 as an open-source project. The money will go into LangSmith, its platform for running, testing and governing AI agents. It works whatever framework or model a tech giant uses.

According to recent reports, the company indicates more than 7,000 organisations use LangSmith. They range from startups such as legal AI firm Harvey, Rippling and Listen Labs to carmaker Toyota, Nvidia and Salesforce. Workday uses it to run and govern agents. That cut Workday’s time to deploy a fresh agent from five months to under a day, LangChain remarked.

“Every organization should be free to choose the best models for its needs, control its data and infrastructure, and continuously improve its agents,” said Harrison Chase, LangChain’s co-founder and CEO.

Chase told the Journal that LangChain’s products aim to make agents’ behaviour easier to control.

“The agent’s behavior is the hard part to control,” Chase stated.

LangChain has 435 full-time staff and aims to grow to 850 by the end of next year, the Journal reported. It also has 47 forward deployed engineers and 13 deployed architects, who work directly with customers. It will hire engineers, researchers, marketers and salespeople with the fresh money.

“It’s an insanely competitive market,” Mo Jomaa, a partner at CapitalG, told the Journal.

LangChain states it will show newly introduced LangSmith features at a release event on 20 November.

7 ways Claude Code can help you run a small business — without writing a single line of code
