For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

    In a recent development, “One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” claims Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them massive. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

    In a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

    In a recent development, beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

    It has been revealed that the burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

    It has been revealed that on Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

    The modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

    In a recent development, what sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

    For instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The company has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

    Beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The tech giant uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

    It has been revealed that further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging looks is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the tech giant’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

    Recent findings suggest that the charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one important difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

    Recent findings suggest that for charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

    Back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

    Sources indicate that then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of latest features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

    In a recent development, apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

    But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

    Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:.

    With Local Lists, Apple Maps consumers in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

    It has been revealed that I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find newly introduced places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

    Industry observers note that even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

    It has been revealed that to find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a upcoming ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

    It has been revealed that trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen reveals only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in Latest York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

    Sources indicate that how does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”.

    It has been revealed that yeah still not my go to navigation option. Until they can give users the amount of information / detail / items to mark and make its alerts functioning like Waze, it won't really be much of a competitor. This stuff if great to have but why Would I want to keep switching between apps to get different information.

    Maybe in 3-5 years their engineering team will mimic Waze and treat it like they've just discovered something great😒🤣.

    Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple states you’ll want to save any places you proposal to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

    Industry observers note that it’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

    You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that indicates when it was last updated.

    Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

    This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.
    • In a recent development, but a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app.
    • It has been revealed that developers know that a massive reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

    In a recent development, but a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so ….

    It has been revealed that developers know that a massive reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

    With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

    Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

    For still photography, I have these:.

    Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

    It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

    Of course, third-party apps still have an vital role, but this one change has made a significant difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

    In a recent development, do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

    Johnny Depp is back on the substantial screen for the first time in years, and he’s playing one of literature’s most famous misers. “Ebenezer: A Christmas Carol,” a darker, gothic reimagining of the Charles Dickens classic from director Ti West, began haunting theaters on November 13, with Depp taking on the role of Ebenezer Scrooge.

    It has been revealed that directed by the filmmaker behind “X” and “Pearl,” the movie puts a darker spin on the familiar tale of a bitter old miser forced to confront his past, present and future over one very notable Christmas Eve. Depp leads a cast of familiar faces like Ian McKellen, Andrea Riseborough, Daisy Ridley, Rupert Grint, and “Severance” standout Tramell Tillman. It’s playing in theaters right now, but how long before you can watch it from the comfort of your own couch?

    Since it just hit theaters, “Ebenezer” isn’t available on any of the best streaming services just yet. Here’s the good news, though: based on Paramount’s recent release patterns, we can make a solid guess about when you’ll be able to rent, buy, and stream it at home.

    If you’re curious about when to start planning for a holiday-centric movie night, we’ve got the answers right here.

    Sources indicate that paramount hasn’t revealed a digital release date yet, but if “Ebenezer” follows the typical pattern for the studio's theatrical releases, it should reach premium video-on-demand platforms about a month after it opens. That means you'll be able to rent or buy it on platforms like Amazon and Apple TV.

    According to recent reports, counting forward from the Nov. 13 release, that points to a digital debut sometime in December 2026, which would make for a convenient rental right around the holidays.

    According to recent reports, physical media releases usually come a few weeks after a film's digital release. Paramount usually puts its films on 4K UHD, Blu-ray, and DVD within a couple of months of its theatrical debut. A disc release for “Ebenezer” around January 2027 seems like a reasonable bet.

    Recent findings suggest that as for streaming it with a subscription, “Ebenezer” has a guaranteed home on Paramount+, since Paramount Pictures movies are on Paramount+. They typically hit the streamer within a few months of their theatrical run, and with this one being a Christmas movie, there’s a good chance Paramount pushes it onto the platform in time for holiday viewing, likely sometime around late December 2026 or into January 2027.

    Sources indicate that that timing could very well change, of course, like Ebenezer's heart. For now, however, the only way to see this holiday tale is to head to the theater.

    Johnny Depp stars as Ebenezer Scrooge, a wealthy, bitter miser who despises Christmas and everyone who loves it. He underpays his employee Bob Cratchit (Rupert Grint), ignores his nephew Fred (Sam Claflin), and is generally unpleasant to be around.

    Seven years earlier, his business partner Jacob Marley (Ian McKellen) died, and now, on Christmas Eve, Marley’s ghost returns to deliver a warning: unless Scrooge changes his ways, he’s doomed to the same miserable fate.

    To give him a chance at redemption, Marley tells Scrooge he’ll be visited by three spirits. The Ghost of Christmas Past (Andrea Riseborough) forces him to relive the memories that turned him so bitter, the Ghost of Christmas Present (Tramell Tillman) shows him how life is right now, including the struggles of the Cratchit family. and the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come offers a horrifying glimpse of what his live will eventually be.

    In a recent development, each haunting pushes Scrooge closer to confronting who he’s become, and to fighting for a second chance at happiness. And if you know the classic story, expect this one to be a little darker.

    #3962. Breaking: The Origins of the Placenta

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Caltech ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The Origins of the Placenta

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caltech

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that when an embryo attaches to the wall of the uterus roughly six days after fertilization, it begins to build the body and placenta.
    • Caltech biologists have now produced the most detailed picture yet of the moment of implantation in mouse embryos, revealing a surprising origin for the placenta.
    • Sources indicate that human embryos appear to have similar cells, which means the findings could help explain why some pregnancies fail very early.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that when an embryo attaches to the wall of the uterus roughly six days after fertilization, it begins to build the body and placenta. Called implantation, this is the stage of life scientists know least about. It is also the stage when most pregnancies are lost.

    Caltech biologists have now produced the most detailed picture yet of the moment of implantation in mouse embryos, revealing a surprising origin for the placenta. It was previously believed to grow from a single group of cells, but by filming embryos as they implanted and monitoring gene activity in more than 22,000 individual cells during and after implantation, the team discovered a second source: a few cells from the opposite side of the embryo that travel to help build it. When these cells were removed, the structure that gives rise to the placenta failed to form.

    Sources indicate that human embryos appear to have similar cells, which means the findings could help explain why some pregnancies fail very early. They also point to what is missing from today's lab-grown embryo models—embryo-like structures made of stem cells—which cannot implant or make a working placenta.

    The research was conducted in the laboratory of Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz, Bren Professor of Biology and Biological Engineering, and appears in a paper appearing in Nature Cell Biology on November 12.

    In a recent development, in the new study, the team combined several approaches to capture implantation as it happens. They identified which genes were switched on in more than 22,000 single cells from mouse embryos at six closely spaced stages. At the same time, they filmed living embryos as they implanted, and tested what happened when specific cells were removed or tracked. The result is a cell-by-cell roadmap of implantation, and it overturns a long-held textbook view of where the placenta comes from.

    In a recent development, before implantation, the mammalian embryo is a hollow ball called a blastocyst. Inside sits a small cluster of cells that will become the body. The outer layer, the trophectoderm, will form the placenta and other support tissues. Scientists divide this outer layer into two regions: the "polar" side touching the inner cluster, and the "mural" side lining the rest of the ball. The accepted model holds that the placenta comes only from the polar side.

    Industry observers note that the Caltech team found otherwise. At the border between the two regions, a handful of mural cells, often just two to four per embryo, behave differently from their neighbors. These "border mural" cells are among the first to touch the uterine wall. They switch on genes associated with placenta-forming cells, then travel upward to join the ectoplacental cone, the structure that goes on to build much of the mouse placenta. These cells' descendants stay in place, on the outer edge of the cone, as the placenta began to form.

    Sources indicate that when the researchers removed most of the mural cells from early embryos grown in the lab, these embryos never formed the early structure that becomes the placenta. In the uterus, very few went on to develop at all.

    "For decades, textbooks have told us the placenta comes from one place," claims Zernicka-Goetz. "Watching embryos implant indicated us that a few cells from the other side of the embryo make the journey too, and that without them the placenta's foundations don't form properly. Our movies of implantation show that these cells are the first embryo-mother contact cells. We hypothesize that this is the contact that primes them to migrate and invade to form the placenta from the top.".

    Recent findings suggest that previous studies have shown that human embryos implant differently from mouse embryos. Even so, when the team filmed human blastocysts in culture, they saw a similar group of border cells moving toward the embryo. A few of these cells switched on the same marker genes the team had found in mice. By analyzing published datasets, the researchers also found cells with this signature among the invasive cells that anchor the human placenta into the uterine wall. This raises the possibility that a comparable population helps build the human placenta.

    The roadmap also revealed other changes that had been hard to see in prior experiments. Just as the embryo implants, the cells that will form the body pass through a brief, distinct state between two known stages of stem-cell development. A gene called Wt1, best known for its role in kidney development and a childhood kidney cancer, switches on sharply at this moment and then switches off again. None of the stem-cell lines that laboratories currently use to model this transition fully capture it. The team also detected the first molecular signs of the head-to-tail body axis earlier than previously reported.

    It has been revealed that scientists can now grow embryo-like structures from stem cells, which are powerful tools for studying early development and infertility. But these models cannot implant properly or make a real placenta. The new results suggest one reason: they lack correctly formed mural cells. "We now hope to be able to establish methods to create these cells in our embryo models with the hope to improve their implantation," Zernicka-Goetz indicates. "If we succeed, these studies might shed new light on why human embryo implantation fail so often.".

    The team has made its full dataset freely available through an interactive website.

    The paper is titled "Mapping mammalian placental formation and implantation transitions with single-cell transcriptomics and live imaging." The study's co-first authors are postdoctoral scholars Dong-Yuan Chen and Wenqi Hu. Additional Caltech coauthors are Shoma Nakagawa, director of the Stem Cell and Embryo Engineering Center; Brian A. Williams, director of the Transcriptome Function and Technology Program; Carol W. Readhead, visiting research scientist; Matt Thomson, professor of computational biology and Heritage Medical Research Institute Investigator; and Barbara Wold (PhD '78), Bren Professor of Molecular Biology and Merkin Institute Professor. Maciej Meglicki of the University of Cambridge is also a coauthor. Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health and the NOMIS Foundation. Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz is an affiliated faculty member with the Tianqiao and Chrissy Chen Institute for Neuroscience at Caltech.

    #3959. The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is my favorite handheld of 2026 and it cures the memory pricing crisis in style

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

    The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is my favorite handheld of 2026 and it cures the memory pricing crisis in style

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Acer Predator Atlas 7 sticks a middle finger up to RAMageddon and strikes the right balance of price, raw performance and efficient software — overcoming a few ergonomic quirks and a smaller battery to become my favorite handheld of 2026.
    • Included matte screen protector fixes glossy display reflections.
    • Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Acer Predator Atlas 7 sticks a middle finger up to RAMageddon and strikes the right balance of price, raw performance and efficient software — overcoming a few ergonomic quirks and a smaller battery to become my favorite handheld of 2026.

    Exceptional Intel Arc G3 performance.

    Significantly cheaper than Z2 Extreme competition.

    Included matte screen protector fixes glossy display reflections.

    Display’s not the brightest or most colorful.

    Dual-fan cooling system gets loud under load.

    Shallow grips have never been my cup of tea.

    Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

    Handheld gaming has become one of the most exciting, yet terrifying, categories in tech. It feels great to have your PC library with you everywhere, but to get there, you either grab something that’s underpowered and overpriced, or you skip rent for a month to get something actually good.

    The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is the rare exception to that rule.

    Industry observers note that at £900 in the U.K. (not available in the U.S. in this base configuration yet), it is a rather unassuming slab of a handheld that hides a monster inside: an Intel Arc G3 chip paired with 16GB of LPDDR5X memory.

    It has been revealed that it easily outmuscles more expensive AMD Ryzen Z2 Extreme competitors while dodging massive component price hikes. And while you will have to manage that smaller 60Wh battery and some loud fans, the sheer gaming grunt for that price makes it my undeniable handheld of the year.

    7-inch HD (1920 x 1080) LCD 120Hz refresh rate.

    1x Micro SD, 2x Thunderbolt 4, 1x 3.5mm audio jack.

    So as I started taking this on solo trips to the pub (yep, I’m that guy) and on my travels all over the place, I started to really see the strengths in the Atlas 7.

    In a recent development, the real superpower is what’s inside: the highly efficient Intel Arc G3 equipped with a B370 GPU and 16GB of LPDDR5X memory. Up until this point, I’d only tested the Arc G3 Extreme, so I was a little nervous heading into its smaller, weaker sibling.

    Turns out, those nerves were unfounded.

    Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

    Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3).

    Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme).

    MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme).

    3DMark Port Royal (ray tracing test).

    The Arc G3 gives you enough breathing room to push your 1080p settings, and sits comfortably above the capabilities of the Ryzen Z2 Extreme in the ROG Xbox Ally X20 — a handheld that’s a third more expensive.

    Plus, when you slap Intel’s XeSS and multi-frame generation on top of a solid baseline frame rate, it feels properly zippy and responsive.

    On a compact 7-inch screen, you don’t see the ghosting or sizzling artifacts that you would on a bigger desktop monitor with the Arc B580 GPU.

    Acer Predator Atlas 8 (Intel Arc G3).

    Asus ROG Xbox Ally X (AMD Ryzen Z2 AI Extreme).

    MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ (Intel Arc G3 Extreme).

    Black Myth: Wukong (1080p Medium).

    There is an anomaly in the Black Myth: Wukong benchmark, but for every other game it was all Intel domination. I think that may be down to optimization for particular silicon.

    On top of that, it is also an extremely capable docked system; Star Wars Galactic Racer ran incredibly smooth at 1440p on medium settings with XeSS set to Performance mode.

    Industry observers note that and don’t get me wrong. You’ll get much more from the Extreme variant, but you’re paying much more to take it up a notch. With the Arc, this much power at this price is right on the money.

    Sources indicate that acer nailed the inputs here. They opted for TMR joysticks, which are incredibly smooth and highly reliable since there are no internal gears grinding away. The face buttons offer a satisfying, tactile clickiness, and while the triggers have a decent amount of depth, I do wish they had a slightly more defined flick to catch my fingers.

    That being mentioned though, this is a nice lightweight system that sees its mass evenly distributed for level playing.

    Windows 11 has finally improved significantly for handhelds. This has been the result of months of work sharpening up the setup process — no more nagging screens asking if you want an Office 365 subscription, just a quick login, some updates and you are ready to play.

    Recent findings suggest that for hardware tweaking, that’s where Acer’s PredatorSense overlay comes in. Pressing the top left button triggers it, and while I’d say Asus’ ROG overlay has a slightly nicer UI, PredatorSense puts all the essential customization settings right within a thumb’s reach without overcomplicating things.

    But to get something together as a value for money proposition, you have to make some compromises.

    The most obvious one is the battery. It’s still sort of decent longevity wise, especially if you get into dropping the TDP to its lowest possible setting and cranking out some indie games. But in our lab test, it’s not great.

    Gaming battery life test result (hh:mm).

    Industry observers note that this surprised me given the effectiveness of those efficiency cores on the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ and its Arc G3 Extreme. But no amount of efficient silicon can overcome a smaller cell.

    Industry observers note that out of the box, the Atlas 7 shares similar ergonomics with the old ROG Ally and Steam Deck, featuring shallower grips that aren’t as ergonomically sound as the chunkier grips on the Ally X20. The end result is a system you’d lean on a table more than comfortably suspended in the air.

    Thermally, the dual-fan cooling system delivers impressive sustained performance, keeping the back of the device nice and cool even at peak output. But the trade-off is noise; those fans do get loud when the system is fully unleashed.

    And finally, the 120Hz display has color and is visible indoors, but the brightness isn’t quite there for playing by a window/strong light source. Plus the glossy finish turns that screen into a mirror, though Acer thankfully includes a matte screen protector in the box.

    The Acer Predator Atlas 7 leaves me conflicted, but in the best way possible.

    For all intents and purposes, this is the best handheld of the year. Yes, there are devices with better displays, chunkier ergonomics and better battery life. But in terms of striking a strong enough mix across all metrics, Acer’s nailed it.

    At £900, it is significantly cheaper than the competition it beats, but I also admit that it's hard to call almost a grand “cheap.” That being mentioned, in the midst of a component crisis where competing devices approach the £2,000 mark with worse performance, the Atlas 7 actually makes you feel like you’re getting your money’s worth.

    Industry observers note that jason brings a decade of tech and gaming journalism experience to his role as a Managing Editor of Computing at Tom's Guide. He has previously written for Laptop Mag, Tom's Hardware, Kotaku, Stuff and BBC Science Focus. In his spare time, you'll find Jason looking for good dogs to pet or thinking about eating pizza if he isn't already.

    iOS 27.3 is coming next month, and during the beta so far there are three latest features I’ve been using almost every day.

    Industry observers note that siri AI in iOS 27 brings major upgrades by providing world knowledge, personal context features, and being more conversational than ever. But one previously revealed Siri improvement—an expanded set of actions for Apple apps—didn’t make the cut in iOS 27.0.

    Now in iOS 27.3, though, Apple is rolling out its first set of newly introduced app actions for Siri AI.

    According to recent reports, siri AI has new capabilities across apps like Calendar, Files, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. It’s a substantial step toward making voice-driven computing more powerful on Apple platforms, and I’ve had fun experimenting with everything new Siri can do.

    Read more: iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many fresh capabilities across Apple apps.

    Apple Health gets a massive overhaul in iOS 27.3, with a fresh design and upcoming features that utilize Apple Intelligence for more personalized health insights. Per Apple:.

    Industry observers note that the updated experience includes a new Insights tab that surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.

    In my testing so far, I’ve especially enjoyed getting up-to-date guidance every day on my health metrics, browsing the deep collection of new educational videos and articles, and understanding all the factors that contribute to longevity. I think Apple is moving the right direction with this upgrade.

    Read more: iOS 27.3 adds all-latest Apple Health app, details here.

    If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, iOS 27.3 adds a powerful new feature called Siri Recap that “ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory.”.

    It has been revealed that "iOS 27.3 adds three latest features I've used almost every day", "Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving". What's with these terrible clickbait titles lately? Did we go back to 2014?

    Siri Recap functions like an outsourced short-term memory reserve. The data it collects is saved inside the Siri app in a fresh Recaps tab, where it lives for seven days and is then deleted—unless you manually save a specific recap.

It reminds me of key details, but there’s nothing I’ve seen that feels overly sensitive or personalized.     #3957. Rust Changed Me as a Developer

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3584 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Startifact ↗ Open Full Page

    Rust Changed Me as a Developer

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Startifact

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1.
    • Recent findings suggest that I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now.
    • Recent findings suggest that what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1. That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty promptly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did.

    Recent findings suggest that I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now. One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did.

    Recent findings suggest that what I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus.

    We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name:.

    Recent findings suggest that the fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak.

    In a recent development, but it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3: the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants:.

    Industry observers note that A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this.

    Recent findings suggest that when you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name. You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other.

    In a recent development, it turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality (null) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error).

    It has been revealed that any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff.

    In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this:.

    The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface.

    According to recent reports, this is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface.

    It has been revealed that let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle.

    But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside.

    Recent findings suggest that or let's say you do want to add a fresh variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog. Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots!

    Recent findings suggest that or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value.

    In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile.

    It has been revealed that enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct.

    Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox.

    In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this:.

    Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html].

    There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled.

    Industry observers note that what if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties.

    According to recent reports, you could create an enum Person; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just mentioned those don't actually exist.

    Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person (Human or Cat) during compile time.

    In a recent development, rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python.

    Sources indicate that in Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is notable.

    Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance.

    Sources indicate that when I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4.

    Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy.

    Obvious: Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working.

    Sources indicate that subtle: Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development.

    Obvious: People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation.

    According to recent reports, subtle: The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development.

    According to recent reports, obvious: Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance!

    Subtle: You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software.

    Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop.

    Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development.

    Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros.

    Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle.

    In a recent development, what if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic!

    Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort, runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust.

    But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time.

    With serde, Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this:.

    With clap, you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enums too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI.

    Recent findings suggest that again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust doesn't normally let you do that.

    How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code.

    According to recent reports, code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That remarked, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too.

    Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a newly introduced class of framework patterns.

    Recent findings suggest that rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel.

    Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box.

    The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust:.

    Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference.

    It has been revealed that this feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it.

    It has been revealed that for circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas.

    In a recent development, A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7.

    Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner.

    Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture.

    A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree, has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot.

    The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference.

    A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere.

    In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do?

    Industry observers note that iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit.

    It has been revealed that fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments.

    interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data.

    the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying.

    Recent findings suggest that rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently.

    In a recent development, I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software.

    Industry observers note that rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction.

    According to recent reports, when you have these tools available, need to develop latest wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8. Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it.

    But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9, it changes how you think. It changes what's possible.

    Industry observers note that sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible.

    Sources indicate that but it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens. But if we open our eyes a little, there are newly introduced architectural possibilities we can explore.

    In a recent development, while the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis: a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar.

    Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up latest areas of opportunity.

    Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enums, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it.

    It has been revealed that rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10.

    AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code, then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more notable to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave.

    If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good.

    You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true/false, or C's enum.

    If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits?

    Recent findings suggest that does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand? Natural language is inherently stretchable.

    It has been revealed that not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do.

    Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts...

    No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way.

    Recent findings suggest that AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself.

    Industry observers note that similar to Grok Bot, Perplexity Teammates are task-oriented proactive agentic AI threads that work for you without constantly being prompted. Meta Muse and ChatGPT Dots are similar, but use a single chat model rather than supporting multiple instances.

    Here’s more about Perplexity Teammates:.

    According to recent reports, teammates are a team of AI agents that own ongoing work. Give a teammate a responsibility, such as managing a growth campaign, triaging incoming bug reports, tracking your metrics, or researching a upcoming market, and it owns that work around the clock. It plans the tasks, brings in more agents when the work grows, and follows through until the result is ready for your review.

    It has been revealed that access to Teammates currently requires a paid Perplexity Max subscription. The feature builds on top of Perplexity’s existing AI orchestration system.

    • “We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

    In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

    “We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

    According to recent reports, “We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”.

    Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz.

    Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

    A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

    Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

    Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw.

    At that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

    Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

    It has been revealed that cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

    Liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré. Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88).

    They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

    Yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

    Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

    Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

It’s quite the coup for Le Rocher given he led Flamengo to their first Brazilian title in five years, the Copa Libertadores and the Copa do Brasil in his 18 months in charge.

    In pre-season so far he has overseen a 5-2 win over fourth-tier AS Saint-Priest, a 2-0 defeat by Sporting Clube, a 2-2 draw with Cercle Bruges and a 1-0 victory over Getafe. They have sold their best player, Maghnes Akliouche, to PSG for £43m and Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m but have so far retained Mamadou Coulibaly and Folarin Balogun, signed and made Ansu Fati’s loan move into a long-term deal.

    Iraola may well persevere with Trey Nyoni in midfield who, after his performances on tour, ought to be on the threshold of a breakthrough season and it would be interesting to see him paired with Ryan Gravenberch just behind Dominik Szoboszlai.

    Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who played well in America after coming on for the injured Joe Gomez, does not have a UK work permit and will have to go abroad on loan for the season but Jérémy Jacquet, who has yet to feature, was due to have a fitness test this morning and would be a welcome to boost to a squad whose defence still requires significant reinforcements.

    Gadgets 📈 Bullish 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

    Epic formally asks SCOTUS to uphold contempt ruling against Apple

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions.
    • As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.
    • The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, epic Games has submitted its official response to Apple’s Supreme Court appeal, urging the justices to uphold the contempt ruling over App Store payment restrictions. Here are the details.

    As most 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple and Epic Games have been engaged in a lengthy legal battle since 2020, when Epic sued Apple after Fortnite was removed from the App Store.

    The move came after Epic remotely activated an alternative payment system that bypassed Apple’s In-App Purchase system.

    Although the court largely sided with Apple, it did rule that the tech giant could no longer prevent developers from directing consumers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

    Apple ultimately allowed those links, but imposed fresh restrictions, including a 27% commission on external purchases, in addition to new rules limiting how developers could display buttons and links to alternative payment methods.

    Epic challenged those restrictions, and the court agreed that Apple had violated the original injunction, holding the firm in civil contempt.

    Apple has since attempted multiple times to overturn that ruling, arguing that the original injunction contained no explicit prohibition on imposing those restrictions.

    Epic, on the other hand, argues that Apple deliberately circumvented the court order by introducing latest rules designed to achieve the same result as those originally prohibited.

    It has been revealed that in May, Apple appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed in June to hear the case. Apple submitted its opening brief in September, followed by supporting briefs from the U.S. government and several legal and business groups.

    Those included the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, Chamber of Progress, and several former federal antitrust enforcers. In a nutshell, the U.S. government argued that the original injunction did not clearly prohibit Apple’s 27% commission on external purchases, but maintained that the tech giant was correctly held in contempt for restricting how developers could display external payment buttons.

    Today, Epic filed its official response.

    In its opening brief, Apple argues, citing multiple legal precedents, that courts must enforce the letter of an injunction rather than its broader spirit.

    According to the organization, there was nothing in the original injunction explicitly prohibiting it from charging commissions on external purchases or imposing additional restrictions on payment links, so it should not be held in contempt for conduct that the court order did not clearly prohibit.

    In its response filed today, Epic disputes Apple’s interpretation of the injunction, arguing that the firm “attempts to avoid contempt by proposing an extreme legal standard.”.

    [Apple] argues that a court can find contempt only if an injunction spells out the exact practice at issue–so an injunction barring Apple’s then-existing anti-steering rules left it free to implement upcoming ones that prevent steering just as effectively. Nothing in this Court’s precedents supports that approach, which would reduce injunctions to a never-ending game of whack-a-mole.

    Epic argues that “Apple devised a plan to circumvent the injunction,” claiming that “Apple chose a rate of 27% for the commission, knowing that, when combined with the developers’ payment-handling costs (more than 3%), the rate for linked-out purchases would be higher than the rate for purchases using Apple’s payment system.”.

    As an Apple executive admitted, every “linked-out transaction is going to be more expensive to any developer * * * than an IAP transaction at 30 percent.” Apple simultaneously commissioned a “sham” report to try to provide an economic justification for the commission; the report contained an “entirely manufactured” rationale for the 27% rate.

    The manufacturer also argues that “Apple tried to cover up its scheme to circumvent the injunction” by asserting privilege over more than 57,000 documents, and points to Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers’ finding that “its Vice President of Finance ‘outright lied under oath’ when he testified about when Apple decided to impose the latest commission.”.

    Finally, Epic asks the Supreme Court to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple or, if the justices decide to clarify the legal standard for contempt, to send the case back to the lower courts for reconsideration under that standard.

    With Epic’s response now filed, Apple has until December 14 to submit its final brief before oral arguments take place on January 11, 2027.

    It has been revealed that coinciding with the launch of Apple HomeView, the manufacturer has been updating its support website with new guides covering everything from facial recognition and user profiles to troubleshooting and repairs. Here are the details.

    Soon after announcing HomeView, Apple published a dedicated support page detailing the device’s repair and service options, including estimated out-of-warranty costs.

    Since then, the company has occasionally published HomeView-related support documents, but the pace has picked up over the past two days, coinciding with the device’s official launch.

    For instance, the Apple HomeView User Guide covers everything from setting up the device and customizing its Home Screen to using Siri AI, managing user profiles, and controlling smart home accessories.

    #3947. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras
