    Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
    • Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
    • In a recent development, the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

    Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

    In a recent development, the sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

    A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

    In a recent development, in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

    Industry observers note that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn rapidly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

    Recent findings suggest that miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

    During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

    And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

    Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

    An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

    Industry observers note that he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

    He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

    A composite sequence of photographs demonstrates the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

    Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

    Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

    On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

    According to recent reports, the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

    To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most key processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

    Industry observers note that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

    As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

    Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

    The European Proba-3 mission, introduced in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

    When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

    It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

    Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

    Industry observers note that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

    According to recent reports, the error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

    Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

    Industry observers note that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

    Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

    It has been revealed that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller states. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

    It has been revealed that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

    The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

    Industry observers note that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

    An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

    “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller states wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

    Recent findings suggest that if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

    In a recent development, on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller indicates with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

    Industry observers note that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” indicates Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

    According to recent reports, as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

    Sources indicate that the countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

    Recent findings suggest that twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

    It has been revealed that among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

    Industry observers note that those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

    Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

    Sources indicate that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

    It has been revealed that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

    “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” indicates Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

    Sources indicate that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

    Recent findings suggest that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

    Sources indicate that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as rapidly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

    The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

    It has been revealed that “The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller claims. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

    The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

    According to recent reports, but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

    “Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller indicates.

    In a recent development, who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Count the subscriptions you’re paying for right now: iCloud, a password manager, a couple of streaming services, a music service, maybe a VPN, and whatever other app decided this year that it needed to be $4.99 per month for something that used to be a one-time purchase.

    Everything is a service now, and a lot of people are hitting the point where one more monthly charge is one too many on principle alone. Cloud storage is the one that’s hardest to cancel, because your photos and files are in it. That’s exactly why pCloud’s Lifetime plans are worth a look this Black Friday: you pay once, and your storage is yours for life!

    In a recent development, apple gives you 5 GB of iCloud for free, which stops being enough about a week after you buy an iPhone. The irony is that they debuted with 5 GB of free storage in 2011, and it’s almost laughable that it hasn’t been increased since.

    After that, it’s a subscription forever. The 2 TB iCloud+ proposal costs $9.99 a month, about $120 a year, for as long as you want your photos to stay where they are. pCloud’s math is different. The 2 TB Lifetime plan is a one-time payment that costs less than four years of iCloud+ at the same size, and the day you buy it is the last day you pay anything for it.

    pCloud has offered lifetime intends for 9 years and now 24 million people use it, and it’s run by a Swiss company under Swiss privacy law. The “what if they go away” question is fair for any lifetime offer, and a company with that track record is the best answer you’re going to get.

    If you’ve been paying for iCloud or Google Drive storage for all of your files for the last 9 years instead of using pCloud, go do the math on how much you’ve spent.

    In a recent development, apple charges a lot to move from a 256 GB MacBook Air to a 512 GB one, and you can’t change your mind later with a hard drive upgrade. Storage has gotten incredibly pricey in recent years as well. pCloud Drive is your solution without breaking the bank. It’s a native Mac app that mounts your pCloud storage as a drive in Finder, so your files appear as if they’re natively on your Mac but live in the cloud until you open them. A 256 GB laptop with a 2 TB pCloud Drive behind it stops feeling small. It runs on macOS, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android, and everything stays in sync across all of them in real time.

    Industry observers note that with pCloud Backup, backing up the folders you choose is easy and safe from a lost laptop, fire, flood, or theft. If you run a NAS at home, pCloud supports backing it up via WebDAV, Rsync, SFTP, and SCP, making it a real offsite destination for a Synology NAS, not just a simple sync folder. It would be a perfect offsite backup for small businesses, remote workers, etc.

    Recent findings suggest that iCloud Photos is great, but it uses storage from your iCloud storage quota, which can get expensive as Apple’s cameras get better and better and file sizes keep increasing. Every pCloud plan includes pCloud Photos, a photo gallery that organizes everything by date on a timeline, automatically tags objects and scenes, and groups shots into albums by event and person.

    According to recent reports, the pCloud mobile app backs up your camera roll automatically to free up space on your iPhone; a Memories feature resurfaces older photos, as the Photos app does; and a built-in document scanner turns receipts and paperwork into PDFs without needing a separate app. Inside the app, there is also a built-in Photo Editor with crop, rotate, brightness, contrast, highlights, shadows, and eight one-click filters, so quick fixes don’t require moving it back to Apple Photos.

    pCloud Docs covers documents, spreadsheets, presentations, PDFs, text, and markdown with six built-in editors and real-time collaboration, all from the browser or the mobile app. If your household is split, with one person on Microsoft, Apple, or Google, pCloud can pull in files from Google Photos, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, and Facebook. That’s the easiest way I’ve seen to get everyone’s files into one place without needing to download and reupload everything.

    In a recent development, files and photos aren’t the only benefit of joining the pCloud ecosystem. pCloud Pass is a password manager that works across all devices, browsers, and operating systems, with one-click login, form filling, and a generator for strong, unique passwords. Passwords are still hard, and most people are either paying monthly for a manager or reusing the same three passwords. A lifetime license solves the annoying aspects of using a dedicated password manager app or being locked into Apple’s or Google’s systems.

    In a recent development, pCloud Encryption is client-side, zero-knowledge encryption for your most sensitive files. In plain language: files in your Crypto folder are encrypted on your Mac before they upload, and only you hold the key. pCloud can’t read them, and neither can anyone else. It’s the right place for tax returns, scans of your birth certificate, and anything else you’d rather not have sitting in a regular sync folder.

    Industry observers note that pCloud’s Black Friday pricing runs from November 13 through November 28. Every plan is a one-time payment with Lifetime access, no subscription, and no renewal.

    lifetime as in lifetime of the tech giant.

    You also get to choose where your data is stored, with data centers in Luxembourg and the United States, and everything is protected in transit with TLS/SSL. With pCloud, it’s your files and your rules, and one Lifetime deal protects everything.

    Industry observers note that if you’re tired of paying for storage every month, this is the week to stop. Grab pCloud’s Black Friday Lifetime deal before it ends on November 28.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

    Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (807 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back.
    • Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.
    • It has been revealed that according to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back.

    Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email.

    It has been revealed that according to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft notes, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact.

    However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted.".

    "The contention matter is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware.".

    The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.

    Recent findings suggest that it was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive.".

    Recent findings suggest that so, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again.

    "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old.

    Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an revision that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored.

    The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity challenges.

    At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in.

    Sources indicate that it is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over.

    It has been revealed that "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report states. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons.".

    Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action.

    By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled.

    However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an update that reverted the defective change.".

    At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update.

    A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An upgrade applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control?

    In a recent development, the engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an enhancement with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ®.

    In a recent development, I’ve spent the past few weeks thinking about how Apple built up the best deal in enterprise AI. Two things happened that make me think Apple knew that all along (or maybe they didn’t and got lucky). Meta released its most capable open-weight model yet and optimized it to run on a Mac Studio. I also spent time with Osaurus, an app that runs a usable local AI model on something as small as a 16 GB Apple silicon laptop without needing a network connection. They even have two models that will run on 8 GB.

    The Xserve has been dead since 2011, but its spiritual successor sits on a desk rather than in a rack.

    In a recent development, about Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

    In a recent development, for the last few years, the narrative has been that Apple fell behind in AI because it didn’t have a frontier model. Siri AI got delayed, and the Apple Intelligence rollout was not great. In hindsight, I think Apple was right not to run that race, as the frontier-model business has turned into somewhat of a capital bonfire. Every frontier lab is spending billions on GPUs to be the best for a few months at a time, and the moment a model is good enough, someone else releases an open-weight version that runs on hardware you already own.

    According to recent reports, open-weight models prove it: Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, 42 billion active parameters, and a million-token context window, and Meta is giving it away. Apple didn’t build that LLM. It built the hardware that runs it. With that being noted, Siri is still far behind.

    In a recent development, look at what Apple has shipped while everyone was waiting on them to try to compete with Anthropic or OpenAI. With Apple silicon’s unified memory, the GPU can use up to 512 GB of memory on a single Mac Studio, instead of being limited to whatever fits on a graphics card.

    MLX is Apple’s machine learning framework, and it’s built specifically for the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon. If you’ve used NumPy, the API will feel familiar right away. On top of that, MLX includes higher-level packages for neural networks and optimizers, along with function transformations for automatic differentiation and graph optimization, so you can build more complex models without giving up efficiency. It also has bindings in Swift, C++, and C, which means it runs on any Apple platform.

    Apple’s own Machine Learning Research post reveals four M5 Ultra Mac Studios running Muse Spark Open at over 36 tokens per second, which is faster than you can read, while peaking around 300 watts per machine.

    Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra’s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

    We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, upcoming features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

    That’s the Xserve pitch, rebuilt for 2026. Apple killed the Xserve in 2011 because nobody wanted a Mac in a data center. The Mac mini came along and provided some upcoming use cases over the years. Now, a couple of Mac Studios can host a model that would otherwise require a rack of Nvidia hardware and a power budget to match, and it does so quietly enough to sit under a desk. Apple wasn’t trying to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, or Nvidia. It was building the infrastructure for everything except the frontier model, and it looks like that’s where the market is going. A tech giant like MacStadium has to be loving this future as well.

    According to recent reports, the Mac Studio story is the headline, but what matters most to most IT teams is at the other end of the lineup. I had Terence Pae, co-founder and CEO of Osaurus, on the Apple @ Work podcast last week. Osaurus is a free, open-source AI tool for the Mac. It helps manage local models that work offline, but it can also call a frontier model when needed. A really cool feature, when it does this, is that Osaurus runs a small local model first to find names, phone numbers, and account numbers in whatever you pasted, and swaps them for placeholders before anything goes to Claude or OpenAI.

    Osaurus has no servers and no customer database. If the organization went out of business tomorrow, the app would keep running until macOS broke it. Individuals use it for free. Workspaces, the paid tier, is for teams who want to share agents across their own Macs. There’s a Windows beta as well, which I think helps Apple’s case more than it hurts it. When the same app runs on both platforms, the Mac’s unified memory is the difference.

    It has been revealed that in talking with him, Terence mentioned he wouldn’t be surprised if a local model matches what today’s frontier models can do by this time next year. I believe him, and that’s the point. The frontier will keep moving, but good enough keeps moving too, and good enough is what most employees need most of the day. Apple spent the AI race building memory, bandwidth, and a framework instead of trying to match the frontier, and the narrative was that they were behind.

    Now the most capable open-weight model in the US is optimized for the Mac.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that bind any C shared library: declare it, wrap functions with defcfn, call them with Clojure values. The db library reaches SQLite and Postgres this way; http-client binds OpenSSL and zlib.

    In a recent development, jolt build ahead-of-time compiles a project (runtime, standard library, app, and its deps) into a single self-contained executable, with C dependencies linked statically. No Chez, no JVM, no source needed to run it.

    Reads Clojure, analyzes it to a host-neutral IR, emits Scheme, and runs it: on Chez natively, or on Gambit compiled to JavaScript. The compiler is written in Clojure and compiles itself; Chez runs interpreted and compiled code identically, so the REPL and a built binary behave the same.

    future/promise/agent/pmap run on OS threads over a shared heap, matching JVM semantics. core.async provides channels and go blocks.

    Sources indicate that immutable vectors (32-way tries), cons lists, and HAMT maps/sets with Clojure value semantics. Transients are real mutable scratch collections.

    Lazy/infinite seqs, transducers, destructuring, multimethods, protocols/records, metadata, namespaces, runtime eval, and the full reader.

    Install the self-contained jolt binary: it bundles the runtime, compiler, and standard library, so there's nothing else to install.

    Or run from a clone (needs Chez Scheme); the bootstrap seed is checked in, so there is no build step:.

    Any C library binds the same way: the native interop guide covers types, memory, structs, and static linking.

    Develop against a live process: see REPL-Driven Development.

    Read the documentation for installation, writing libraries, and C interop.

    Industry observers note that jolt targets Clojure semantics but runs on Scheme, not the JVM. Most portable Clojure runs unchanged: persistent collections, the numeric tower, lazy seqs, transducers, multimethods, protocols/records, atoms, future/agent/pmap, core.async, runtime eval, and the full reader all behave as on the JVM.     Industry observers note that 9. Raising Cane’s — Best chicken-tender specialist.

    8. Wendy’s — Best mainstream all-rounder.

    Industry observers note that 7. Shake Shack — Best premium burger option.

    6. Popeyes — Best for bold chicken flavor.

    5. Taco Bell — Best for variety and customization.

    In a recent development, 4. Jersey Mike’s — Best sandwich chain.

    3. Chick-fil-A — Best dependable chicken stop.

    2. In-N-Out Burger — Best focused burger menu.

    Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t expecting Panda Express to make an appearance on a list of the best fast food restaurants. And as someone who was severely disappointed by Raising Cane’s the first time I had it, I was taken aback to see it get a mention on ChatGPT’s list. As for the rest of the chatbot’s choices, they all made sense to me. At the top of ChatGPT’s ranked list was Culver’s, which it marked as the best overall. Its reasoning for selecting that fast-food chain as the absolute best centered around it meeting all of the chatbot’s specific standards (value, consistency, menu variety and service):.

    ButterBurgers, cheese curds, and frozen custard make a compelling combination, and the broader menu gives families plenty of choices. It earns first place because the whole meal feels considered, from the main course through dessert. ACSI’s 2026 study also highlights its made-to-order food and friendly service.

    Gemini’s list was determined by four main benchmarks: food quality, consistency, value and overall customer satisfaction. And just like ChatGPT, its top 10 was impacted by the same benchmarks measured by the American Customer Satisfaction Index. Gemini’s choices also took general customer sentiment of each fast-food spot into account.

    Sources indicate that this time around, a different restaurant received the honor of being chosen as #1, while ChatGPT’s top selection got knocked down to #3. Here’s how Gemini’s rankings looked from 10 to two:.

    Gemini gave valid reasons for each of its picks, such as In-N-Out Burger’s peak freshness when it comes to its made-to-order food, fair pricing practices and respectable menu choices. It even mentioned the “Double-Double Animal Style” cheeseburger as the standout item on its menu. As for which fast-food chain emerged as #1, it turned out to be one that I frequently go to during my lunch breaks:.

    Chick-fil-A. The Reason: Consistency and hospitality set the standard here. Even with massive drive-thru volumes, order accuracy and speed are best-in-class. The Standout: The classic pressure-cooked, peanut-oil-fried chicken sandwich, waffle fries, and house Chick-fil-A sauce.

    Claude stepped up to the (deep-fried) plate to offer its rankings, which were determined by each restaurant’s food quality, consistency, value, service, and signature approach to making food. It also considered customer satisfaction surveys and the general reputation of each fast-food chain when listing its picks.

    After taking a quick peek at its honorable mentions (which included Shake Shack, Panda Express, Jersey Mike’s and Dunkin’), I came away slightly shocked by two of its choices (since they weren’t mentioned by ChatGPT and Gemini) and less surprised by the other picks that made Claude’s list:.

    According to recent reports, when I glanced at which fast-food chain earned the top spot on Claude’s list, it ended up being the very same place that Gemini chose: Chick-fil-A. Claude’s explanation as to why it also chose that spot is as follows: It consistently tops customer satisfaction surveys. The chicken sandwich is reliably good, service is fast and friendly even with long drive-thru lines, and restaurants are unusually clean and well run.

    And for the final ranked list of the finest fast-food establishments, Perplexity considered its choice based on the following criteria: food quality & flavor, value, consistency, menu distinctiveness and convenience. Here are the restaurants that got a mention on Perplexity’s list, from 10 to two (it was funny to see Perplexity agree with Gemini’s choice for the tenth spot):.

    To my surprise, Chick-fil-A didn’t earn another top spot—Perplexity was far more enamored with In-N-Out Burger as the best fast-food chain in America. And as for why it chose that option, it highlighted the following reason:.

    Industry observers note that my best overall choice for a focused burger experience. Its appeal is a tightly defined menu built around burgers, with customizations such as Animal Style adding variety without turning it into an everything-for-everyone chain. Time Out also ranks it No. 1. Start with a Double-Double, Animal Style.

    According to recent reports, gemini and Claude agree that Chick-fil-A is second to none in the competitive race for who makes the best fast food in the nation. ChatGPT chose Culver’s as its fast-food champion, while Perplexity went in a completely different direction by choosing In-N-Out Burger as the top-of-the-line fast-food restaurant. Seeing my personal faves, such as Zaxby’s, Bojangles and Cook Out, get excluded from their lists was a total bummer, but I can see how they may pale in comparison to their more recognizable competitors.

    Even though there’s no Culver’s or In-N-Out Burger located in my home state of New York, I’ll be sure to celebrate National Fast Food Day by stuffing my face with some Chick-fil-A (that new chicken & waffles sandwich is everything it’s been hyped up to be and more).

    Breaking: Here’s a HomeView feature that should come to every Apple device

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home.
    • According to recent reports, on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time.
    • In a recent development, with HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This week, Apple started shipping the HomeView, its first display made for the smart home. On the HomeView, there’s one particularly nice feature that I’d love to see make its way to all Apple platforms: Ambient Dark Mode.

    According to recent reports, on iOS, iPadOS, and macOS today – the only flexibility you have on dark mode is whether or not it automatically switches on towards night time. While this is generally helpful and certainly appreciated, it isn’t super granular. Of course, you can adjust the time when it switches, but generally speaking its just a one time toggle.

    In a recent development, with HomeView, you can enable ambient dark mode. In display settings, once you enable automatic dark mode, there’s the usual two settings you’d see on other Apple platforms: sunrise to sunset, as well as a custom schedule. HomeView takes it a step further with ambient mode, where the ambient light sensor determines whether or not you should be in light or dark mode.

    Industry observers note that of course, a sunrise to sunset schedule generally works for most cases. However, if you’re up late at night with your lights turned on, you still might prefer light mode in an instance where macOS would generally be in dark mode. Similarly, if you wake up later in the day with your curtains shut, at say 11am, you might not want to immediately see light mode on your phone the second you open your eyes.

    There are tons of good reasons for why someone would prefer ambient light-based automatic light and dark mode switching. HomeView software is the first Apple platform to enable this, and I’d love to see it come to iPhone, iPad, and Mac starting next year with OS 28.

    #3935. Tech Report: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

    📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2972 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.
    • Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.
    • According to recent reports, last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Japan’s MMX mission aims to sample the Martian moon Phobos.

    Japan's MMX spacecraft will fire its engines to slow down and enter orbit around Mars.

    According to recent reports, last August, looking up from the edge of an ancient river delta on Mars, the Perseverance rover’s electronic eye spied an oblong shadow crossing the distant, glowing Sun. Phobos, the Martian moon named for the Greek god of fear and panic, was transiting the solar disk. Too small to darken the pale, dust-tinged sky, but orbiting close enough to eclipse a significant fraction of the Sun, Phobos passed in less than a minute.

    NASA’s Perseverance rover captured Phobos passing in front of the Sun from the surface of Mars.ASU/MSSS/SSI/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

    The tiny moon, with its murky origins, is an enigma, and one whose makeup and history could tell us much about Mars and the wider solar system. And now the international Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, which successfully debuted on 20 October, seeks to explore that mystery with an unprecedented series of landings on the unknown surface of Phobos.

    Industry observers note that this mission brings unusual challenges—for example, designing an orbit to study a microgravity moon orbiting a much larger planet. Engineers also had to figure out how to assess and land on this low-gravity pile of loosely assembled dirt and rock, how a rover might rove across it, and how the spacecraft might take samples and return them to Earth.

    Industry observers note that “I often say that landing on Phobos is like trying to land a balloon,” claims Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager of MMX at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). “It’s very difficult to drop a balloon to the ground and prevent it from tilting or bouncing.”.

    Phobos is one of two small Martian moons; the other is Deimos, named after the Greek god of dread and terror. Their cosmic origins are unknown, though there are two prevailing theories. One holds that the moons were once asteroids from the belt between Mars and Jupiter, captured by the smaller planet’s gravity. In the other theory, Phobos and Deimos formed when a large celestial body slammed into Mars, sending debris into orbit. Some models suggest the pair are the last survivors from a cluster of satellites.

    The enormous Stickney crater, roughly 9 kilometers across, dominates this view of Phobos taken by NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.University of Arizona/JPL-Caltech/NASA.

    Scientifically speaking, Phobos is considered a rubble pile, a loosely consolidated aggregate of rock and dust. Far too small to become spherical under its own mass, it’s shaped like a lumpy potato, roughly 27 kilometers in length, with only 1/1,800th of Earth’s gravity. On Phobos, a typical adult would weigh about as much as a tennis ball does on Earth.

    More than 10 years in the making, MMX rolled out on Japan’s flagship H3 rocket from Tanegashima spaceport on 20 October local time. It will arrive at Mars in 2027 carrying scientific payloads from several space agencies, including NASA, and a fresh rover called Idefix developed by the French and German space agencies (CNES and DLR) in collaboration with JAXA.

    Engineers assembled MMX’s modules at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center before the spacecraft’s October 2026 launch.JAXA.

    Recent findings suggest that MMX consists of three modules: a propulsion module to power its journey to Mars and apply the brakes to enter orbit around the red planet; an exploration module carrying the rover, sampling gear, and other scientific instruments; and a return module, attached to the exploration module, that harbors the capsule destined for a high-speed reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. After collecting samples on Phobos, the exploration and return modules will lift off together. The exploration module will then be jettisoned while the return module sets a course back home.

    Industry observers note that if all goes according to blueprint, MMX will deliver a 10-gram sample to Earth in the second half of 2031. But the mission will face a series of daunting challenges to reach that end point, including navigating complex orbits around Phobos and landing on its surface while Mars periodically blocks communications with Earth.

    The MMX’s modular design includes the propulsion module [left] and the exploration and return modules [right].Kyodo News/Getty Images.

    “It’s the most complex mission I have ever seen,” claims Patrick Michel, director of research at CNRS (the French National Center for Scientific Research) and co-principal investigator on Idefix.

    An H3 rocket carried MMX into space on 20 October 2026, beginning the mission’s five-year journey to Phobos and back.The Asahi Shimbun/Getty Images.

    Recent findings suggest that once MMX reached low Earth orbit, its propulsion module’s engine fired, kicking off a nearly year-long deep-space cruise to Mars. On arrival, the spacecraft will need to fire its engines in an extended, carefully timed burn to slow down enough to be captured by Mars gravity. The propulsion module will then be jettisoned, leaving the exploration and return modules to orbit Mars.

    “If something doesn’t go according to strategy, MMX will fly by Mars and get catapulted into the solar system,” notes Nicola Baresi, an astrodynamicist who coauthored a paper on specially designed orbits for MMX.

    Industry observers note that from that initial orbit, MMX will transition into a specially designed quasi-satellite orbit that allows it to keep pace with the small moon but also move around it. Since Phobos is too small to orbit in the conventional sense, the spacecraft will orbit Mars alongside the moon, following a clever egg-shaped path that slings MMX alternately ahead of and behind the moon. “When you’re closer to Mars, you’re accelerating with respect to Phobos, and when you’re farther from Mars, you’re decelerating. So you essentially go back and forth,” explains Baresi.

    Martian Maneuvers To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.Chris Philpot.

    To reach Phobos, MMX will execute three major maneuvers: MOI-1 will put the spacecraft into orbit around Mars, MOI-2 will transfer it toward Phobos, and MOI-3 will place it into its final orbit alongside the moon.

    It has been revealed that the best existing images of Phobos, from spacecraft such as NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and ESA’s Mars Express, have resolutions of only a few meters per pixel. That’s larger than Idefix, the mission’s rover, itself about the size of a microwave oven. To map the surface in greater detail, MMX will loop in front of and behind Phobos at distances ranging from 200 kilometers to less than 20 km from the surface.

    During its two-year remote sensing campaign, the exploration module will use several cameras and a laser altimeter to map the surface in high resolution and look for candidate landing sites. When Mars passes behind the Sun as seen from the Earth, causing a roughly two-week communications blackout, MMX will retreat into a larger, stable orbit. After communications resume, MMX will prepare to send its first visitor down to the surface.

    Before the exploration and connected return modules attempt to land, Kawakatsu indicates, MMX will send a scout that in Japanese is called “the first penguin,” leaping into unknown waters. For this mission, the first to leap will be the Idefix rover, named for the canine companion to Obelix in the French comics series Asterix. The exploration module will release the rover during a low-altitude pass of between 40 and 100 meters above Phobos’s surface in 2028 or early 2029.

    MMX will use its TENGOO camera [left] and LIDAR laser altimeter [right] to map Phobos’s terrain.JAXA.

    According to recent reports, it will be a tense moment that calls back to 2005, during Japan’s Hayabusa mission to explore the asteroid Itokawa. In a similarly designed drop, the MINERVA rover was released from an orbiter, but erroneously at 200 meters instead of the intended 70 meters. The rover missed the asteroid and, without propulsion, drifted off into deep space.

    Idefix will get a slight nudge out of the exploration module toward its negligible-gravity target, freefalling and likely tumbling as it goes. It’s expected to touch down with a velocity of less than 1 meter per second. Unlike rovers that have landed on other surfaces with airbags or dedicated landing legs, Idefix will land without protection, apart from some extra padding on the solar panels due to their critical nature. The barely-there gravity of Phobos should allow the 23-kilogram rover to land softly, though exactly how this landing will play out is hard to predict.

    The Idefix rover will travel to Phobos with its wheels tucked in and solar panels folded.DLR.

    In a recent development, “It will bounce probably several times,” notes Stephan Ulamec, Idefix’s co-principal investigator and project manager at DLR. “It will come to rest somehow in some position.” Once it’s still, four retracted legs will deploy to right the rover autonomously, regardless of its orientation. It will then unfold its solar panels to charge its batteries for exploration tasks ahead.

    Sources indicate that A simulation indicates how Idefix is expected to tumble onto Phobos, right itself using its articulated legs, and begin exploring the moon’s surface. DLR.

    Once operational, Idefix will roll at a snail’s pace, topping out at one millimeter per second. Its metal wheels have protruding blades like a paddle wheel, designed to gain traction in Phobos’s microgravity. “If we were to drive our rover faster, then it would actually be more like we were swimming through instead of driving across the surface,” claims Cecily Sunday, a doctoral student involved in testing Idefix’s WheelCams at the Institut Superieur de l’Aeronautique et de l’Espace (ISAE-Supaéro) in Toulouse, France.

    The WheelCams, a pair of cameras placed on the underside of the rover, will observe the wheels and their tracks during Idefix’s planned 100-Earth-day primary mission. The images will help researchers study the size and distribution of grains in Phobos’s regolith and how cohesive they are. How much or how little the grains stick together will greatly impact how Idefix moves. Sunday likens this to the difference between driving on dry and wet sand. “Think of trying to build a sandcastle with dry sand,” she says. “You can’t. Add water, and suddenly you can.”.

    The Idefix rover was mounted between the MMX spacecraft’s landing legs for the journey to Phobos.DLR.

    Recent findings suggest that the team tested the rover’s nine-bladed wheels on a variety of materials, including Phobos regolith simulants provided by JAXA and DLR, lunar simulants, glass beads, quartz sand, and clay pebbles. “We characterize the mechanical properties of each simulant precisely, then test across the full range, with varying grain size, angularity, and even color, so we can map what we see in the WheelCam images back to actual surface properties,” Sunday indicates.

    Sources indicate that despite the microgravity and Phobos’s rubble-pile nature, Sunday says Earth-based tests can approximate the rover’s motion on the surface of the small moon fairly well. While Phobos’s reduced gravity lowers the rover’s effective weight, there is also reduced pressure between the grains beneath its wheels. “As long as you’re moving very, very slowly and using the same materials and the same weight of the system, they should be representative,” Sunday says.

    With four paddle-like wheels and deployable solar panels, Idefix is designed to crawl across Phobos.Ardan Fuessmann/Imago/Alamy.

    Idefix’s interactions with its fresh home will offer “sub-millimeter resolution and information on porosity, on grain size, on surface strength, on how hard is the material,” Ulamec says. “It fills a gap between remote observations from orbit and detailed observations of the return samples back on Earth.”.

    It has been revealed that what Idefix finds on this rocky, rugged world will help determine how and where JAXA attempts to land the main spacecraft. Michel notes the touchdown will provide ground truth for understanding of Phobos. When NASA’s OSIRIS-REx spacecraft touched down on the asteroid Bennu to collect a sample, its sampling arm surprisingly sank nearly half a meter into the loose material. But Ulamec doesn’t think Idefix will sink deep into Phobos, noting that Bennu is very different and much smaller, with a diameter of 500 meters.

    In a recent development, once Idefix has investigated the surface, MMX will face an even greater challenge: landing its much larger exploration module on Phobos. The spacecraft will make a controlled descent to roughly 10 meters above the surface, then drop the remaining distance in free fall. With so little gravity to pull it downward, even a small sideways motion could cause the lander to tip or bounce away. A successful, upright landing would mark the start of up to two hours on Phobos for the crucial sampling phase.

    It has been revealed that the MMX mission draws on the experience and technologies of Japan’s two Hayabusa sample-return missions, which landed on the asteroids Itokawa and Ryugu. But this mission has many more moving parts. MMX’s exploration module will use two sampling devices—a coring sampler developed by JAXA and a pneumatic sampler provided by NASA and fabricated by Honeybee Robotics, a subsidiary of Blue Origin. Data from these tools, and those carried by the Idefix rover, could answer questions about the origin of Phobos and how the Mars system has evolved.

    Industry observers note that the coring sampler uses a robot arm and a cylindrical corer designed to reach at least 2 centimeters below the surface. The arm can maneuver to find the best site for digging. “That by itself is a challenge because we’ve never done it,” Michel claims. “You never know what can happen at the very sampling site itself, where you might have a boulder and the arm cannot move.”.

    Probing beneath the top layer will be valuable because solar radiation, galactic cosmic rays, and micrometeorites have battered and weathered the surface. The material below should offer a better record of the moon’s origins, and JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of it.

    MMX will carry both the Idefix rover [bottom] and a robotic coring sampler [top] designed to dig beneath Phobos’s weathered surface.JAXA.

    It has been revealed that the pneumatic sampler takes a different approach. Mounted on one of the lander’s legs, it will inject pure, non-reactive nitrogen gas into the surface and capture the grains stirred up. This sample could illuminate the changes Mars and its moons have undergone over time. The dual system also adds redundancy in the face of Phobos’s unknowns. “If the surface of Phobos proves to be very hard, [the coring sampler] may struggle to penetrate the ground. [The pneumatic sampler] would not experience this glitch and still be able to gather material,” Kawakatsu claims.

    One of the most intriguing aspects of MMX is the additional possibility of collecting material from the planet below. It’s likely that Phobos has been peppered by Martian ejecta thrown into space by meteor impacts, so MMX also provides an opportunity to return the first Martian samples to Earth. Michel estimates that the samples could contain “a few hundred grains coming from Mars.” Scientists can distinguish those grains from native Phobos material by analyzing their oxygen isotopes.

    That possibility raises a planetary-protection question. A direct Mars sample-return mission would have to follow strict rules to ensure that potentially living biological material from Mars doesn’t contaminate Earth. But those protocols don’t apply to MMX, even if its sample does collect grains of Martian soil. A panel of experts concluded that any microbes blasted off Mars wouldn’t survive the violent impact and ejection or the intense radiation exposure on the way to Phobos. This saved MMX from implementing expensive and time-consuming quarantine and containment protocols for the returning sample.

    After landing on Phobos, MMX will have roughly two hours to collect samples from the moon’s surface before lifting off again.JAXA.

    Sources indicate that during the brief surface operation, the robotic arm will deposit the samples in a storage unit, from which they’ll be transferred into a capsule aboard the return module and sealed in a vacuum. After that, lift off.

    Once back in Mars orbit, the exploration module will resume its observations of Phobos and make several flybys of Mars’s other diminutive moon, Deimos, to gather data on its surface, structure, and composition. In November 2030, during a favorable alignment of Mars and Earth, MMX will begin the homeward leg of its trip. The return module will separate from the exploration module and power the voyage home, its sole objective to bring the dust of Phobos to Earth.

    MMX’s sample return capsule will carry material from Phobos through Earth’s atmosphere in 2031.JAXA.

    According to recent reports, finally, in 2031, the 60-centimeter-wide sample capsule will plunge into Earth’s atmosphere at roughly 12 kilometers per second. Assuming it survives the extreme heat of reentry and lands safely in Australia, scientists will begin to tease out clues about Phobos and the early solar system. JAXA’s Institute of Space and Astronautical Science will receive and curate the samples, which will also be shared with mission partners.

    “We have macroscale measurements from the spacecraft, microscale measurements with the rover, and then sample analysis,” Michel indicates. “So we can relate the three kinds of scales together because we have all of them.” The insights gleaned from orbital images, close-up images of the regolith, and the chemical analysis of the samples could have wider implications for our understanding of our solar system.

    Industry observers note that “MMX is a mission to understand the Mars system and shed light onto how terrestrial planets like the Earth, and maybe Mars, develop a habitable environment,” Kawakatsu states. “We strongly suspect that our terrestrial planet region formed dry, and water and organics were scattered inwards from the icy-rich outer solar system.” Mars, he says, sits at the gateway between the inner and outer solar system, making its moons valuable witnesses to the processes that shaped potentially habitable worlds.

    #3933. Industry News: Doctor reveals one of the most common triggers for waking up at night — and how to fix it so that you start sleeping through again

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1298 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Doctor reveals one of the most common triggers for waking up at night — and how to fix it so that you start sleeping through again

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Brief awakenings are a normal part of sleep, but constantly waking up at 3 a.m.
    • Recent findings suggest that while everyone's experience with night-time awakenings are different, research has shown that there some common causes for disrupted sleep.
    • Sources indicate that "You might not even realize you're thirsty until you're wide awake, but by then, the quality of your sleep has already taken a hit," says board-certified internal medicine physician Dr.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Brief awakenings are a normal part of sleep, but constantly waking up at 3 a.m. and being unable to fall back asleep can be a cause for concern. While it's clear that middle insomnia can lead to poor health and low energy levels, what isn't so clear is why we wake up in the middle of the night.

    Recent findings suggest that while everyone's experience with night-time awakenings are different, research has shown that there some common causes for disrupted sleep. The U.S. Sleep Hygiene Report by MattressNextDay surveyed 1,500 Americans across all 50 US states and found that the top reason for middle insomnia is thirst, with 36% of respondents sharing that they wake up at night because they need a drink.

    Sources indicate that "You might not even realize you're thirsty until you're wide awake, but by then, the quality of your sleep has already taken a hit," says board-certified internal medicine physician Dr. Danielle Wall, M.D.

    To find out why thirst disrupts sleep and how to fix it, I've called on Dr. Wall and Sammy Margo, a physiotherapist and resident sleep expert at Dreams. So, read on to find out what's behind your nocturnal need for a glass of water, plus how you can keep thirst at bay throughout the night.

    Recent findings suggest that research highlights that there is a strong link between dehydration and shorter, fragmented sleep, with Dr. Wall telling me we should think of thirst as a "biological wake-up call".

    Sources indicate that "When you're dehydrated, your brain triggers a response to get you to find water, which effectively pulls you out of your sleep," explains Dr. Wall, Sit 'n Sleep's resident medical reviewer.

    The doctor warns that waking up for a glass of water disrupts our sleep cycles, which then prevents us from getting enough "deep, restorative rest".

    Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

    Chartered physiotherapist Margo says that cutting deep sleep short impacts your readiness to face the day ahead, too.

    "These interruptions may make it harder to enjoy a continuous, restful night's sleep, potentially leaving you feeling tired and less refreshed the following morning" warns Margo.

    The physio and the founder of The Good Sleep Expert also highlights that thirst can make it difficult to fall back asleep once you've woken up at night.

    "When you're dehydrated, your body may struggle to regulate its temperature, while your heart rate may also increase, making it harder to relax and drift off back to sleep," she points out.

    It may seem obvious that night-time thirst is caused by a lack of hydration.

    What's less obvious is that hydration should begin as soon we wake up if we want to fight off nocturnal awakenings — not from gulping down a glass of water before bed.

    "In many cases, it's just a matter of catching up — you haven't had enough water during the day, and your body realizes it once you settle in," says Dr. Wall.

    Studies have found that room temperature has a huge effect on hydration levels, with warm environments over 81°F (27°C) increasing the risk of dehydration.

    "If your bedroom is too warm, you may find yourself sweating more than usual, causing your body to lose additional fluids and potentially leaving you waking up feeling thirsty," explains Margo.

    "With the colder weather, many of us are also turning up the heating, but this can contribute to dry air, leaving you waking up with a dry mouth or throat," she adds.

    Sources indicate that according to Dr. Wall, our night-time awakenings are not just about our water intake (or lack thereof); it's also about what we eat.

    "High-sodium or high-sugar dinners draw water out of your cells, which spikes that thirsty feeling," notes the physician.

    Margo also says that spicy foods can play a role in 3 a.m. wake-ups.

    It has been revealed that “Spicy foods can also increase your body temperature at a time when your body is naturally trying to cool down for sleep," she explains. "They can also contribute to indigestion or acid reflux, making it harder to get comfortable and drift off.".

    While studies now show that various drinks, from soda to coffee, contribute to our daily hydration levels, that doesn't mean we should be drinking them close to bedtime — especially alcohol.

    “It's also no secret that alcohol can contribute to dehydration, and with Christmas party season approaching, having a few drinks in the evening may leave you feeling particularly thirsty overnight," says Margo.

    It has been revealed that dr. Wall agrees: "I always warn against alcohol in the evening; while it might help you drift off, research shows it actually dries you out and disrupts the quality of your REM sleep.".

    While lifestyle habits, from food intake to a glass of wine in the evening, can cause night-time dehydration, illness and medical conditions can also play a role.

    In a recent development, "We see waking up feeling thirsty with mouth breathing, whether it's from a stuffy nose or sleep apnea; it dries out your mouth and throat very quickly, leaving you feeling parched," explains Dr. Wall.

    Both sleep experts agree that the best strategy for preventing night-time thirst is to get the bulk of your fluids in early.

    "I'd recommend starting your day with a glass of water and drinking regularly throughout the morning and afternoon, rather than waiting until you feel thirsty," advises Margo. "Keeping a water bottle nearby can be a helpful reminder to sip throughout the day.".

    Drinking the lion's share of your fluid intake in the morning can also help stave off nocturia, too.

    "To avoid those frustrating middle-of-the-night bathroom runs, start tapering off your drinks about two or three hours before you strategy to go to bed," suggests Dr. Wall.

    For dinner, Dr. Wall indicates it's best to skip alcohol and limit high-sugar desserts that, according to research, can affect your blood sugar and make you thirstier.

    "I'd suggest avoiding anything heavily processed or salty, like canned soups, salty snacks, or processed meats, because salt triggers an almost immediate need for water," the doctor advises.

    Instead, she tells me that we should be opting for lighter meals and hydrating foods. "You can also eat water-rich foods like cucumbers, celery, or watermelon," she says.

    In a recent development, while Dr. Wall recommends keeping your thermostat around 65°F (18°C) to prevent fluid loss from a too-warm bedroom, she also indicates using the best bed sheets, such as those made from cooling percale and Tencel, can help, too.

    "Using breathable, natural fibers like cotton or linen for your sheets and pyjamas helps your body stay cool and wicks away moisture," claims the board-certified doctor.

    "If the air in your room is particularly dry, a humidifier can also keep your nasal passages from drying out," she adds.

She is interested in the relationship between sleep and health, interviewing an array of experts to create in-depth articles about topics such as nutrition, sleep disorders, sleep hygiene, and mattress care.
