    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that in September, Apple introduced the new Beats 360 headphones, the first overears from Beats since the Beats Studio Pro in 2023. That stated, the older Beats Studio Pro still remain on sale at a lower price point – so it begs the question, which Beats headphones are more worthwhile?

    Industry observers note that one of the biggest differences between the two will be the price. The Beats Studio Pro, since they’re older, are regularly available on discount. Right now, you can pick up Beats Studio Pro for $199-249 on Amazon, compared to Beats 360, which aren’t discounted from their $349 launch pricing.

    It has been revealed that despite being older and cheaper, the Beats Studio Pro have a couple advantages over the Beats 360. On top of the fact that they’re $100-150 cheaper, you may very well still want to consider them.

    According to recent reports, the biggest advantages, in my view, have to do with the form factor. The Beats Studio Pro can fold down into a much more compact size, whereas Beats 360 don’t fold at all. This means it’s easier to carry around the Beats Studio Pro.

    In a recent development, beats Studio Pro also offer a headphone jack, whereas Beats 360 don’t have any sort of wired audio at all, even over USB-C. This means Beats Studio Pro are easier to use in environments where bluetooth audio isn’t convenient, such as with a game console or on an airplane.

    Sources indicate that one of my favorite things about the Beats 360 is that they offer UltraPlush cushions you can swap into, but those cost extra. Beats Studio Pro by default come with UltraPlush cushions, so you can have a more comfortable experience out of the box.

    Industry observers note that of course, Beats 360 are newer, so by default they do a number of things better. That includes:.

    According to recent reports, out of everything on this list, I’d say clearer transparency, stronger noise cancellation, and automatic device switching make the biggest difference. In my testing, its hard to hear with the transparency mode on the Beats Studio Pro, so I end up taking the headphones off to have conversation. With Beats 360, that isn’t the case.

    As for noise cancellation and automatic device switching, I feel that if you’re buying Beats for the sake of having Apple headphones, you should buy the ones that offer true automatic device switching – and those are the Beats 360. Noise cancellation is more of a personal preference, but if you value having the best noise cancellation, the Beats 360 are noticeably better.

    It has been revealed that lastly, the Beats 360 do have the customizable design going for them. While customization is more aesthetically pleasing, it also has an advantage longer term – when the earcups start wearing down over the years, you can rapidly replace them on the Beats 360.

    Sources indicate that while it’s hard to overlook the fact that Beats Studio Pro come in at a much lower price point, I’d generally say that if you want a great pair of headphones that offer an Apple experience, you probably shouldn’t buy the Beats Studio Pro. The Beats Studio Pro are a fine pair of headphones for the price, but you certainly aren’t getting all of the same ecosystem creature comforts that Beats 360 offer.

    That remarked, Beats 360 simply do not offer a headphone jack or a foldable design, and if those things matter to you, then Beats Studio Pro might still be the way to go. Beats Studio Pro also offer a ton of different color options that aren’t available on Beats 360, while costing $150 less.

    The stock market continues to grapple with volatility amid geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. Given this uncertainty, investors looking for steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

    Tracking the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick the right dividend stocks, as these experts assign their ratings after an in-depth analysis of a tech giant's financials and ability to pay dividends consistently.

    Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

    Downstream energy company Phillips 66 (PSX) is this week's first dividend pick. With a quarterly dividend $1.27 per share (annualized dividend of $5.08), PSX offers a yield of 2.25%. The company recently reported solid Q2 earnings, as the Middle East conflict affected global supplies and drove up refining margins.

    Following the Q2 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Phillips 66 and raised his price target to $255 from $240, reflecting higher 2026 earnings expectations and lower interest expense next year.

    According to recent reports, gabelman highlighted the quarter-over-quarter reduction in Phillips 66's net debt, noting management's optimism at achieving its estimated $15.5 billion net debt target one year ahead of schedule. The 5-star analyst expects the organization to end 2026 with a net debt of $14.6 billion.

    "The [balance sheet] improvement could re-establish PSX as a go-to defensive refiner," said Gabelman.

    Industry observers note that management agreed that PSX's payout ratio lagged year-to-date, but expects buybacks to increase in the second half. Gabelman remarked Phillps indicated the possibility of a larger dividend hike following an annual increase of 5% over the past two years.

    Sources indicate that gabelman ranks No. 554 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Phillips 66 Statistics on TipRanks.

    Crescent Energy (CRGY) is an exploration and production organization with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian and Uinta Basins. Earlier this month, the company reported better-than-expected Q2 earnings and declared a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share, payable on August 31. At an annualized dividend of $0.48 per share, CRGY boasts a dividend yield of about 4%.

    According to recent reports, in reaction to Q2 results, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reaffirmed a buy rating on Crescent Energy stock with a price target of $18. He noted continued strength in the firm's performance, with second-quarter oil production and cash flow surpassing the Street's expectations.

    "CRGY's cash flow exceeded expectations by 10%, reinforcing its trajectory of capital efficiency," said Richardson.

    According to recent reports, the 5-star analyst highlighted that Crescent raised its full-year oil production guidance, citing the effective integration of the Vital Energy acquisition. Specifically, Crescent tripled its synergy target from the Vital Energy deal to as much as $300 million, significantly reducing the effective purchase price. This reflects Crescent's solid execution following the acquisition, Richardson noted.

    Additionally, the analyst noted that Crescent's capital spending is and heading toward the lower end of management's prior guidance, indicating disciplined financial controls.

    According to recent reports, richardson ranks No. 579 among more than 12,400 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.5%. See Crescent Energy Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

    Finally, Viper Energy (VNOM) is effectively controlled by Diamondback Energy. Viper owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests in oil-weighted basins, mainly the Permian in West Texas. Viper recently announced its Q2 2026 results and declared a 32% hike in its base dividend, effective in the third quarter of 2026. The fresh base dividend indicates a 4.5% annualized yield.

    Industry observers note that viper also removed its quarterly commitment to return at least 75% of cash available for distribution. The company believes that this move will ensure increased flexibility to make opportunistic share repurchases and pursue accretive mergers and acquisitions.

    Industry observers note that following the Q2 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper, slightly raising his price target to $59 from $58. Bilkoski said Viper's solid Q2 performance supports his view that the strength in oil prices and rising operator activity are driving higher production.

    According to recent reports, "Viper has delivered, and we forecast will continue to deliver, one of the highest production per share growth profiles in our royalty universe" through the end of 2027, stated Bilkoski. He believes Viper deserves a premium valuation, given its above-average growth.

    Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Groundworkcollaborative

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events.
    • The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale.
    • Recent findings suggest that groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events. The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts, examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier.

    The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales.

    Recent findings suggest that groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page indicates, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.”.

    Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens, shared the following reaction:.

    Sources indicate that “Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette.

    “Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.”.

    Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then indicates how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that every now and then, a product hits the Tom’s Guide testing lab that hooks me the second I start testing it.
    • As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip.
    • When I posted about my switch on social media, people thought I was crazy to ditch a large, laptop-replacing tablet for a smaller screen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that every now and then, a product hits the Tom’s Guide testing lab that hooks me the second I start testing it. That’s exactly what happened with the iPad mini 8.

    As a 12-inch iPad Pro with M1 chip owner, three features on the iPad Mini instantly won me over: the vibrant OLED screen, the compact footprint, and the power of the A20 chip. Paired with a solid trade-in offer for my older Pro, I couldn’t resist the urge to get one for myself.

    When I posted about my switch on social media, people thought I was crazy to ditch a large, laptop-replacing tablet for a smaller screen. They were wrong.

    In a recent development, after picking up the iPad mini and using it daily for a week, I’m left asking myself why I bought the iPad Pro in the first place. The mini is, hands down, the perfect tablet for how I actually live and work.

    Buying new products from Apple can get expensive, so when I saw Apple increase its trade-in values ahead of the iPad mini 8's launch, I decided it was the perfect opportunity to upgrade. Apple offered me $440 for my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro, bringing the cost of a fully specced-out iPad mini down to around $660 (without the nano-texture display).

    That was the biggest selling point for me, but I could have saved even more by opting for a lower-tier configuration with the standard 128GB of storage, which would have brought my out-of-pocket cost closer to $350. Getting a new iPad with a faster processor and a better OLED display for that kind of money felt like a steal.

    Sources indicate that when I first bought my 12-inch M1 iPad Pro back in 2021, I was looking at it as a potential laptop replacement. I didn't own a MacBook at the time, so as a Windows user, the iPad became my go-to device for many of the things I now do on my Mac, including sending iMessages and making FaceTime calls.

    Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

    It's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to.

    That changed when I bought a 16-inch MacBook Pro with an M3 Max chip just two years ago. Suddenly, I wasn’t on Windows all the time, and I had a much more capable laptop.

    Even before that, though, the 12-inch iPad Pro wasn't exactly the most comfortable device to take everywhere. It's smaller than a MacBook, but adding the Magic Keyboard gave it some serious heft. Holding it for extended periods or balancing it on my lap to watch YouTube videos and stream movies could also get awkward. My hands would get tired, and its size meant I often needed a case just to prop it up at a comfortable viewing angle.

    The iPad mini is a completely different experience. Its smaller footprint makes it much easier to use with one hand, and I can comfortably rest it on my lap while watching movies or catching up on videos. When I was playing *The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time*, on my Nintendo Switch 2 for example, it was the perfect size to keep on my lap while following online guides and navigating puzzles.

    Sources indicate that it's a strange thing to say, but the smaller iPad finally made me feel like I was using an iPad the way I was supposed to. Rather than trying to replace my laptop, it feels more like a convenient and natural extension of the Apple and non-Apple devices I already own.

    In the week I've had it, I've started carrying my iPad mini everywhere. It slips easily into my bag, whether I'm using it as a second display with Sidecar or keeping it alongside my work laptop as a convenient companion device. That's something I never really felt compelled to do with my old iPad Pro.

    One of the biggest reasons I was willing to give up my iPad Pro for the iPad mini was the display. The new iPad mini features a fantastic OLED panel, and my colleague Tony Polanco goes into more detail about what makes it so impressive in his review. For me, though, the upgrade was in a similar scope.

    In a recent development, whether I'm watching YouTube videos or streaming shows like Chicago Fire on Peacock, the iPad mini's OLED screen is a huge step up from the Mini-LED display on my older iPad Pro. While it doesn't get quite as bright, I spent enough time reviewing TVs to appreciate just how much more vibrant and color-accurate the OLED panel makes my favorite shows look.

    Take Chicago Fire, for example. The flames pop with rich reds and oranges, while skin tones look noticeably more natural. Even finer details, like the soot and ash on firefighters' faces, come through with impressive clarity and depth.

    That's not to say the iPad Pro had a bad display, but the iPad mini's OLED screen is simply in another league when it comes to watching movies and TV reveals.

    It has been revealed that and before you ask, I really don't miss the iPad Pro’s 120Hz refresh rate. For watching videos and handling everyday tasks, the difference between 60Hz and 120Hz isn't particularly noticeable. I can spot it when scrolling through websites or swiping around the home screen, but outside of those moments, I rarely think about it.

    In a recent development, I mentioned earlier that the iPad mini finally feels like an iPad I'm comfortable using as a companion to my other Apple devices. But out of curiosity, I decided to see how well it could handle the kind of work I used to do on my older iPad Pro. After all, with an A20 Pro chip under the hood, this is still a seriously capable tablet despite its smaller size.

    In a recent development, much to my surprise, the iPad mini handled it just as well as my M1 iPad Pro. When I connected it to the Apple Studio Display in our lab, I was able to arrange apps in windows and use the monitor as an extended display. I even managed to get through a full workday this way, entering data into spreadsheets in Google Sheets Chrome, responding to Slack messages, and switching between Safari and Microsoft Edge.

    Industry observers note that it's pretty remarkable that such a small tablet can handle this kind of desktop-style workflow, especially when the iPhone Duo, despite featuring the same chip, can't do the same. Considering that extended-display support and windowed multitasking were once features largely reserved for iPads with Apple's M-series processors, it's impressive to see them make their way to a smaller, more affordable tablet.

    After a week with the iPad mini, I can honestly say I am glad I traded in my iPad Pro. What started as an opportunity to get a great trade-in deal turned into a much bigger upgrade to how I use my iPad.

    In a recent development, the smaller design makes it far more comfortable to carry around and use, while the OLED display is a massive improvement for watching movies and TV reveals. And despite its compact size and A20 chip, the iPad mini is surprisingly capable when I need to get some actual work done when connected to an external monitor.

    It has been revealed that of course, there are compromises here that you’d want to keep in mind if you want to go my route. The screen is much smaller than the iPad Pro, and the lack of a 120Hz refresh rate might be noticeable for some people.

    But those are trade-offs I'm more than willing to make for a tablet that's easier to take everywhere and genuinely enjoyable to use.

    I bought the iPad mini because Apple's trade-in offer made it an incredibly tempting deal. But after using it for a week, I think I've discovered something more vital: I just need an iPad to be a great iPad. And with that, this tiny Apple tablet is great.

    #3924. Software is breaking down at a systemic level

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2615 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Breck-mckye ↗ Open Full Page

    Software is breaking down at a systemic level

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breck-mckye

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?
    • This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.
    • Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it?

    This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States.

    Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems.

    And then there was the eMudhra fiasco, where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical.

    Sources indicate that it’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here?

    Sources indicate that you might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours.

    I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely.

    Sources indicate that but AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it.

    Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other.

    According to recent reports, the Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic.

    Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage.

    Industry observers note that microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism:.

    Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned.

    Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs.

    His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture.

    According to recent reports, on October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website. Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers.

    In a recent development, it turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites.

    The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify.

    Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some vital packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM).

    These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream.

    When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens.

    The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies.

    According to recent reports, any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code.

    In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything.

    It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry.

    Industry observers note that building software was hard. Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely upcoming and different.

    It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand.

    But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money.

    Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much.

    Recent findings suggest that about ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries.

    Industry observers note that cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic.

    According to recent reports, companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops.

    And then, we had the Open Source boom.

    It has been revealed that it was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json, hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet.

    Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever.

    This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it.

    Industry observers note that open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t).

    Industry observers note that but the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble.

    Industry observers note that because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists.

    This changed the balance of power between workers and management.

    It has been revealed that imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage.

    Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong.

    By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points.

    The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects.

    But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor, technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe.

    According to recent reports, A lot has been written about how AI systems are inherently non-deterministic, a kind of slot machine that only creates simulacra of work. Acting like a stochastic parrot, this argument goes, AI generated code will always be prone to hallucinations and bugs.

    Industry observers note that and there’s truth to that. But I think the danger in the present moment is the opposite. It’s not so much that the model outputs are crap and unreliable. They’re actually pretty good at doing what you ask them to do (though I suspect that mostly works because Anthropic and co heavily subsidise compute).

    I think the real AI threat is decoherence.

    Kristen Maevyn wrote an essay named The Decoherence Trap which talks about a problem where the individual parts of a system may look fine in isolation, but don’t make sense as part of a larger system.

    Decoherence: the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects.

    Software engineers, as I’ve seen them working over the last year, have all but turned over all their work to AI agents. It started with small tasks like writing tests, functions, and individual components. But now it’s everything - not only the components, but the design, the orchestration, the whole concept.

    Programming was the activity of translating ideas and intents from the messy human world into code so crystalline, so precise and pedantic, that even a computer could execute it. It was fundamentally the act of distilling complexity into order, making something real out of nothing.

    This activity is rapidly dying. It no longer happens in most tech companies.

    In a recent development, most SWEs now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent - they just can’t keep on top of the complexity. Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels - we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.

    In a recent development, decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a newly introduced phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable.

    A form of learned helplessness has emerged, along with a paradoxical false confidence, caused by the ways LLMs provide the illusion of work without actually forcing us to think through the details.

    This de-skilling of software engineers only shifts the balance of power even further away from developers - who can no longer raise the alarm. At its worst, AI turns tech workers into “meat proxies” who spend their days massaging prompts and letting Claude figure out if the work is actually complete.

    According to recent reports, it’s not just programmers. It’s the whole chain, top to bottom. Everyone is using AI, especially in significant tech.

    According to recent reports, claude generates code because the engineer wrote a prompt. The prompt comes from a ticket that was written with Claude. The project manager wrote the ticket based on a summary of a document, that was written by, and then summarised back, by Claude. The document uses statistics from a calculation, by Claude. The business is panicking about the stock market, and the stock market prioritises short term trends over long term engineering.

    According to recent reports, does this sound accurate? It’s a caricature, but not by a lot.

    I believe that tech companies risk losing their “organisational cognition” - their ability to think and respond as a coherent unit.

    Industry observers note that this is the real threat: a scenario where nothing in the system is done with intent, and nobody in the system has control. We generate complexity faster than we can tame it.

    Look at the problems I’ve outlined. They are about systems of excessive complexity, made of parts that need to work perfectly or else everything falls apart. These parts are being individually corroded by corner-cutting, cost-cutting, overcomplication, over-reliance on uncompensated work and - I fear - helplessness amongst the people who build digital infrastructure.

    It has been revealed that this is a threat to all of us. The tech industry is now critical to everyday life. It’s the software that controls your flights, your banking, your petrol pumps, your TV, your payroll. It’s what allows you to navigate roads and find your friends. It’s how you date and how you eat. It’s how you’re reading this.

    Society has extended trust, too much trust, into technical systems that are now demonstrating systemic deterioration. I do not think society, government, or institutions are prepared for a world where the incidents and outages of 2026 become commonplace. They too are extending the chain of dependencies, assumptions, complexity and unwarranted trust. Each layer, each link in the chain is a upcoming point of attack that can subvert everything on top of it.

    The internet is at a breaking point. The software we build is not legible enough to bear the responsibility the world is giving it. We are telling ourselves the AI revolution is succeeding, precisely because of the rate at which we are generating complexity. The actual load-bearing parts of the ecosystem - open source, engineering-led judgement - are crumbling away.

    I think we are only at the beginning of a very painful phase. This is not a blip, and it’s not an aberration - it’s the new normal.

    It has been revealed that the current MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip, which is the same chip used in the iPhone 16 Pro. As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is working on a next-generation MacBook Neo powered by the A19 Pro chip.

    In terms of performance, the A19 Pro is about 10-15% faster than the A18 Pro in single-core and multi-core CPU tests. The jump in GPU performance is even bigger, with benchmarks showing an up to 40% boost for the A19 Pro. This is because every GPU core in the A19 Pro has Neural Accelerators built in.

    The A19 Pro chip is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone Air.

    According to recent reports, according to reporter Tim Culpan, Apple will likely use a “binned” version of the A19 Pro chip in the MacBook Neo. While the A19 Pro chip in the iPhone 17 Pro has a 6-core GPU, the MacBook Neo version of the chip will likely have a 5-core GPU.

    It has been revealed that one of the compromises of the MacBook Neo is that it has 8GB of RAM. The rest of Apple’s Mac lineup nowadays starts with 16GB of RAM.

    According to recent reports, the next-generation MacBook Neo won’t jump all the way to 16GB of RAM. Instead, it’s expected to offer 12GB of RAM thanks to the aforementioned A19 Pro.

    As I wrote in my review, I don’t think it’s a huge limitation that the MacBook Neo has just 8GB of RAM. Still, an increase for the next-generation model is a great improvement.

    According to recent reports, the combination of the A19 Pro chip and 12GB of RAM upgrades should also unlock support for Apple’s more powerful on-device AI model declared at WWDC. This model enables a more accurate dictation experience and upcoming options for customizing the Siri voice.

    The current MacBook Neo doesn’t support this feature because of its A18 Pro chip and 8GB of RAM.

    According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is available in an array of fun colors, including citrus, blush, indigo, and silver. Bloomberg reports that Apple’s blueprint is to “periodically” patch the MacBook Neo with latest colors.

    There aren’t any details on which colors the next-generation MacBook Neo will be available in.

    According to recent reports, apple released the current MacBook Neo in March. Tim Culpan reports that the A19 Pro version of the machine is slated for a release sometime in 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that she is not alone. Across North America and Australia, thousands of communities have used oversize roadside sculptures to put themselves on the map.     Tyra’s fate hangs in this balance.

    Sources indicate that last year, the Drumheller and District Chamber of Commerce decided to close Tyra’s site when its land lease expires in 2029, citing unsustainable maintenance costs. The decision set off a scramble to determine her future.

    Recent findings suggest that for a quarter-century, tourists have stepped out of their cars near the intersection of Gorgosaurus Street and Tyrannosaurus Drive to snap photographs of Tyra. The bravest visitors climb 106 steps to peer out from between her fiberglass teeth to views of the Canadian Badlands.

But this new K4 Air by Kuxiu might be the most impressive option I’ve tested to date. This charger is just 8.5mm thin, weighs less than 120 g, and can wirelessly charge your iPhone at up to 25W. And even though they went ultra-slim, they did not really need to sacrifice any charging performance. You get:.

    Industry observers note that one of my favorite things about Kuxiu has always been their price-to-performance ratio. While some brands and companies are removing charging bricks and even cables, Kuxiu is adding a ton of value here by including everything you need directly in the packaging. The build quality of the charger is also fantastic. It feels balanced, well-made, and extremely versatile because of all the situations you can use it in.

    Kuxiu has also done a great job of bringing us a Burgundy color option that perfectly matches the fresh Burgundy iPhone color. I wish Apple would continue making the Cosmic Orange iPhone because the K4 Air in that orange would have been awesome.

    Recent findings suggest that I recommend watching our video to see my reaction when I pick up the K4 Air for the first time. I was shocked at how small it was. The form factor and size make it incredibly easy to throw into any bag, pocket, purse, or even just leave it attached to your iPhone for when it is needed.

    Sources indicate that the charging experience is actually pretty straightforward. You unfold the charger, connect the USB-C cable, and you’re ready to go. The main magnetic charging surface supports your iPhone, while the second surface is for AirPods. They even added magnets to the AirPods charging pad to ensure they stay in place every single time. There is also a dedicated Apple Watch charger that folds down to charge any Apple Watch. I was charging my Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it fit perfectly.

    According to recent reports, but now the big question: how well does it work with the iPhone Duo? Personally, I charge my iPhone Duo on my nightstand charger when it is folded shut. So I have zero problems with it. But if you open the iPhone, place it on the charger in landscape mode, and then use it, it will tilt slightly to the left. But to my surprise, if you use the iPhone Duo and open it in portrait mode, it works great! The charger doubles as a stand and easily supports the iPhone Duo. Another cool piece that the form factor unlocks is that it can technically charge two iPhones at the same time, so if you are in a pinch, you can charge two iPhones at once,.

    So, regardless of which iPhone you are using, as long as it supports MagSafe, you are good to go. But how much does something like this cost?

    The Kuxiu K4 Air is finally back in stock after a limited initial run. You can get it on Kuxiu’s website for $79. It comes in Space Gray and their new Burgundy color. As I mentioned above, you also get the charging cable, a 45W charging brick, and a carrying pouch.

There are a ton of great 3-in-1 chargers, with latest ones flooding the market daily, but very few combine this level of portability with all the features we discussed.

    So if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your massive three Apple products, and looks fantastic.

    #3916. Industry News: Michael Mann's 'Heat' Copyright Fight Turns on a Deal with Himself

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1987 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Copyrightlately ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Michael Mann's 'Heat' Copyright Fight Turns on a Deal with Himself

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Copyrightlately

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, upcoming Regency indicates the director can’t reclaim rights in “Heat” because he wrote it for his own company.
    • Industry observers note that the most famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat is a six-minute cup of coffee.
    • A lawsuit filed Friday in Los Angeles federal court describes a similar meeting.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, upcoming Regency indicates the director can’t reclaim rights in “Heat” because he wrote it for his own company. Mann says he wrote the early drafts on his own, not as his loan-out’s employee.

    Industry observers note that the most famous scene in Michael Mann’s Heat is a six-minute cup of coffee. Al Pacino’s cop and Robert De Niro’s thief, sharing the screen for the first time, sit across a table and discover they’re more or less the same guy.

    A lawsuit filed Friday in Los Angeles federal court describes a similar meeting. According to New Regency’s complaint, Mann is trying to reclaim rights in his early Heat screenplay drafts based on a 1988 deal in which Michael Mann met with Michael Mann and assigned those drafts to two companies he controlled. Nobody wrote anything down. The studio states Mann only recently “discovered” the alleged oral agreement with himself “after forgetting about it for nearly four decades,” and that when it asked for proof, his story changed.

    But first, to see why this lawsuit landed now, we need a bit of the Heat 2 backstory.

    In a recent development, mann published Heat 2, a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner, in 2022. According to the complaint, Upcoming Regency then licensed the sequel film rights to one of Mann’s companies. Warner Bros. came aboard in 2023 to co-produce, and Mann delivered a script in March 2025. Warner Bros. reportedly balked at Mann’s $170 million budget and let him shop the project elsewhere. In October 2025, the trades announced that Amazon MGM’s United Artists was picking up the project, with Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale set to star. Asked about the move at a festival in Lyon, Mann told reporters, “I can’t get into all the politics of it.”.

    In a recent development, the complaint gets into some of those politics. Latest Regency states Warner’s license reverted to it when the studio passed. Then, on April 29, 2026, months before the Amazon agreements described in the complaint were signed, Mann served New Regency with a notice purporting to terminate its rights in Heat. Two more termination notices followed in May.

    Recent findings suggest that amazon’s apparent response was to buy the sequel rights twice. According to the complaint, Mann granted Amazon in October whatever Heat 2 rights he “may personally recapture” under his termination notices, and a few days later, New Regency granted Amazon “certain of” its own rights. Both agreements acknowledge the dispute, and some of each side’s promises about title to the Heat screenplay depend on how it comes out. It’s like buying insurance from two companies, each of which insists the other’s policy is worthless.

    Newly introduced Regency sued on November 13. Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the case is “unrelated to production of Heat 2,” which is scheduled to start shooting January 19. With agreements from both sides, Amazon may be covered for the sequel either way, though the complaint claims nothing about what comes after it.

    A quick refresher for anyone who skipped my last few articles on this (it’s fine, they were long).

    Now add the loan-out company. Hollywood writers and directors commonly work through corporations they own, which formally employ them and lend their services to studios (hence the name). If you write a screenplay as an employee of your own company, the company is the legal author. It can’t terminate, because it’s a company. You can’t terminate, because you’re not the author. And even when the artist is the author, courts haven’t let artists terminate deals their loan-outs signed. As the judge in John Waite’s case put it, “people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes—e.g. taking advantage of tax benefits—and then disavow it for others.”.

    Industry observers note that so Mann needs three things: a piece of Heat he wrote as himself, a grant of that piece that he made personally, and a link between that grant and the rights Newly introduced Regency actually holds. New Regency says he has none of them.

    Sources indicate that heat took almost twenty years to reach the screen, and Upcoming Regency says Mann called his writing a work for hire at every step. The complaint lays out the paper trail. In 1976, his new loan-out, the Michael Mann Company, lent his services to Columbia Pictures for a TV crime project. In 1989, the paperwork for an NBC movie called L.A. Takedown recited that he wrote the teleplay as “an employee-for-hire” of the loan-out and “reserved no rights.” And in 1994, the loan-out sold Warner Bros. the Heat screenplay as material Mann wrote “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed for the company and again for himself.

    According to recent reports, but none of those agreements dates from 1981 to 1985, and that’s the period Mann is focusing on. According to the complaint, Mann now says he wrote early Heat drafts in those years on his own, as what New Regency calls “an unemployed author.” (That window covers Thief, The Keep and the launch of Miami Vice, so as unemployment goes, it was a pretty productive stretch.) Mann’s spokesperson told Variety the dispute concerns “original and personal writing Michael Mann did on multiple screenplays during the 1980s.”.

    In a recent development, that’s different from the argument made by Road House writer Lance Hill, who calls his loan-out an “alter ego” that should be disregarded for purposes of termination. Mann, as Newly introduced Regency tells it, accepts that his loan-out was real. He just claims he wasn’t working for it at the time he wrote the good stuff.

    It has been revealed that next Mann needs a personal grant. His first termination notice identified an October 1, 1988 agreement with two companies he controlled: his loan-out and ZZY, Inc. Newly introduced Regency states that when it asked for a copy, Mann’s lawyer explained there wasn’t one, because the agreement was oral. When the studio pressed for evidence, it says, the loan-out dropped out of the deal. A second notice followed, this time identifying an agreement between Mann and ZZY alone. New Regency likens Mann to “a Shakespearean actor playing multiple parts.”.

    Sources indicate that the third termination notice concerns a written 1989 agreement assigning L.A. Takedown material to another Mann firm, Ajar, Inc. The complaint states the rights Mann assigned personally came from an earlier Columbia project, which was never produced and which he may have reacquired under a Writers Guild agreement. Latest Regency replies that reacquiring rights doesn’t change authorship: if the 1976 project was Columbia’s work for hire, it still is.

    So altogether, Mann has served three termination notices aimed at two different grants. Nearly all of this is New Regency’s version of events. Mann hasn’t yet answered the complaint, and his spokesperson has noted only that he’s “exercising the right of authors to reclaim their work and in this case Michael Mann’s original creation.”.

    The strangest thing about this case is that Mann is trying to terminate a grant that, by New Regency’s account, nobody can document. Why not the 1994 Warner Bros. agreement, which is in writing?

    I can think of a couple of reasons. First, that deal was made by his loan-out, which assigned the screenplay as material Mann wrote for it “as a work made for hire.” Mann signed too, but only to be personally bound “to the extent necessary,” which isn’t the same as granting rights himself. That’s John Waite’s problem all over again. Then there’s the calendar. Even if Mann could terminate the 1994 deal, he couldn’t do it before December 2030. A 1988 grant, on Mann’s reading, gets him there in 2028.

    But even if an oral grant can be terminated (Newly introduced Regency indicates it can’t, because it was never “executed”), what does Mann get back? An exclusive license or transfer of ownership requires a signed writing, so the most ZZY could have received via an oral conversation was a nonexclusive license. New Regency says its exclusive rights come through the 1994 deal, not through ZZY. Ending a nonexclusive license to ZZY wouldn’t touch rights that reached New Regency some other way. So Mann could win the termination fight and still not get back what he actually wants.

    The larger prize may come after Heat 2. In July, TheWrap reported that Amazon is already exploring Heat 3, and that the franchise’s long-term value was part of why it took on the sequel. If Mann succeeds in reclaiming rights that Newly introduced Regency presently controls, he could have real leverage over future Heat projects, while New Regency would keep the 1995 film and whatever was added to the story after those early drafts. Depending on what Mann actually gets back, neither side may be able to make another Heat movie without the other, which would put them in the same spot as Pacino and De Niro at the diner: across a table from each other, with a lot to talk about.

    New Regency looks to have a strong case, at least on the facts we have now. But not because Mann supposedly made a deal with himself. Contracting with yourself is the whole business model of a loan-out, and New Regency is the one insisting the court respect Mann’s.

    Mann has a plausible answer to the work-for-hire argument. He doesn’t appear to be saying his loan-out was an artifice or should be disregarded, but rather that the work at issue was written outside of it. A court could agree without blowing up anybody’s tax returns. And the work-for-hire labels aren’t conclusive. In August 1994, Mann signed a certificate declaring that everything he had “heretofore or hereafter” written relating to Heat was a work made for hire. But in Marvel Characters, Inc. v. Simon, the Second Circuit held that simply calling a work “made for hire” after the fact doesn’t make it one. So a certificate signed in 1994 isn’t necessarily determinative of what actually happened in 1982.

    In a recent development, the difficulty for Mann is proving it. “Outside my employment” is hard to show when writing was your job. Two years after Simon, the same court held in the Martha Graham case that dances Graham created while employed full-time to choreograph belonged to her employer, however much creative freedom she had.

    And the paper trail here may defeat Mann’s theory in any event. According to Latest Regency, in the 1989 Ajar agreement, signed less than six months after the supposed oral deal, Mann warranted that the “Hanna” rights hadn’t been transferred to anyone, even though his first notice describes the work he orally assigned as “Heat a/k/a … Hanna.” And while Mann can argue the work-for-hire language was boilerplate, he’ll have to explain why it appears in agreements spanning nearly two decades, some of which he signed twice. (Then there’s the question I raised in 2023: if his best writing fell outside his employment, what exactly was his loan-out getting? The IRS might find that as interesting as a federal judge does.).

    Even if Mann clears all that, he still has to connect a 1988 oral grant to rights that, by New Regency’s account, came through the 1994 deal. The picture could change once Mann answers the complaint and the early drafts surface. Until then, New Regency’s documents beat Mann’s memory.

    Sources indicate that robert De Niro’s character in Heat, Neil McCauley, lived by a rule against getting attached to anything he couldn’t walk out on in thirty seconds. Mann has been attached to Heat for fifty years and to his loan-out for just as long, and this case may force him to choose between them.

Whether that's down to the cost, the lengthy wait times, or the issues with broken screens, is unclear.     #3913. The upcoming Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

    📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (572 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

    The upcoming Apple TV has twice as much RAM as the previous model, but apps and games can’t use it

    📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The upcoming Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version.
    • It has been revealed that however, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves.
    • Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The upcoming Apple TV 4K features an A19 chip inside with 128 GB storage and 8 GB RAM, twice the amount of memory as the previous version. Presumably, the supply crunch surrounding the memory chips is part of the reason this generation of Apple TV box jumped to a $299 price point as well.

    It has been revealed that however, although the specs have been upgraded, apps and games are not actually able to use more RAM for themselves. Apps on Apple TV are limited by the operating system to 2 GB RAM each, and that cap has not changed on the fourth-generation box.

    Obviously, most of the apps you run on Apple TV are streaming service clients, which generally have much smaller RAM requirements anyway. However, ostensibly, Apple markets the Apple TV as a gaming device and RAM constraints matter much more there.

    A hypothetically graphics-intensive game will easily hit the 2 GB RAM ceiling, and some fans had hoped that the upcoming box with the new chip and double the internal memory would help here. Unfortunately, with the current tvOS software, that is not the case.

    Recent findings suggest that 9to5Mac independently confirmed that an Apple TV app is force-quit by the system when it allocates more than two gigabytes of memory for its process. The developer API os_proc_available_memory function also reports a 2 GB limit to the app, the same value as the third-gen Apple TV.

    Recent findings suggest that it is unclear whether this is an intentional policy decision, or an oversight. Nevertheless, the 2 GB limit is the status quo. Tangentially, it’s worth noting that the 128 GB of onboard storage is also not usable by a single app or game; tvOS imposes app bundle limits of about 4 gigabytes with apps able to reserve about 20 GB extra for some assets.

    Regarding the unchanged RAM limit despite doubling the internal memory on the chip, there is some speculation that Apple opted to reserve a portion of the system memory to help the performance of the Siri AI models. However, this doesn’t make too much sense to us. The most complex Siri AI features you can do on the TV offload to a connected iPhone or server backend anyway. The same Siri AI features are also available on the prior two generations of Apple TV hardware, so it doesn’t seem like RAM constraints are a meaningful factor.

    Sources indicate that one group of customers hoping for more RAM in the Apple TV was the game decomp community, which use AI to get AAA studio games running on anything from an Apple TV to an iPhone. Some of their projects have run into the 2GB tvOS limit previously, and were hoping that the fresh Apple TV would alleviate that. So far, that is simply not the case.

    Industry observers note that next fall, Apple will introduce its second-generation iPhone Duo.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

    According to recent reports, that noted, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an glitch.

    Right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

    One of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

    In a recent development, so, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

    Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

    Recent findings suggest that this would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to promptly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

    #3908. How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

    📅 25 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2537 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Interceptsuite ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Intercept HTTP/3 Traffic: QUIC and Qpack

    📅 25 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2537 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Interceptsuite

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP.
    • It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge.
    • Recent findings suggest that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that short answer: HTTP/3 does not go through an HTTP proxy, because it runs over QUIC, and QUIC runs over UDP. Most HTTP proxies, such as Burp Suite, are built on HTTP over TCP, so they never see it. To intercept HTTP/3 you need a proxy that can relay UDP and can act as a man in the middle for QUIC. After that, the work is about streams and header compression: the request is not text any more, it is bytes on a QUIC stream, compressed with QPACK.

    It has been revealed that in this post we intercept real HTTP/3 traffic from curl and from Microsoft Edge. Then we use a small lab server to look at every byte, so the QUIC and QPACK parts are easy to follow.

    Recent findings suggest that this post uses InterceptSuite, so you should know what it is and what it is not. It is not built for HTTP. It is built for raw network traffic: TCP, TLS, UDP, DTLS and QUIC. Because it can intercept UDP and QUIC, it can handle HTTP/3 too. But it does not come with an HTTP parser, and that is also true for HTTP/3. The core shows raw bytes.

    To read and edit those bytes as HTTP, InterceptSuite has an extension API, and there is an official, open source HTTP/3 extension that decodes the QUIC stream and QPACK headers into text. You can read the code, change it, or send a fix. The decoding in the screenshots below comes from that extension, not from the core.

    If you have only used HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, three things are different.

    According to recent reports, 1. It runs on QUIC, not TCP. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP carried over QUIC (RFC 9000). QUIC packets travel inside UDP datagrams. TLS 1.3 is part of the QUIC handshake (RFC 9001), so there is no separate "TCP then TLS" step.

    In a recent development, 2. The client has to learn that the server speaks HTTP/3. The ALPN name for HTTP/3 is h3. A server can advertise it with an Alt-Svc response header, and a DNS HTTPS record can advertise it too (RFC 9460). So a browser often makes its first request over TCP, then moves to QUIC.

    According to recent reports, 3. Everything is a stream. A QUIC connection carries many streams. The two lowest bits of a stream ID tell you what it is (RFC 9000, section 2.1):.

    In a recent development, in HTTP/3, every client-started two-way stream is one request and its response (stream 0, 4, 8 and so on). The one-way streams are for housekeeping: a control stream, and two QPACK streams. Their type is the first byte on the stream: 0x00 control, 0x02 QPACK encoder, 0x03 QPACK decoder (RFC 9114, section 6.2 and RFC 9204, section 4.2).

    It has been revealed that one more detail that matters for interception. The first packets of a QUIC connection (the Initial packets) are protected with keys that anyone can calculate from the connection ID, so they have no real secrecy (RFC 9001, section 5). That is why a passive observer can still see things like the server name in the handshake. Everything after the handshake is encrypted with keys from the TLS 1.3 exchange. You cannot read it without being one of the two ends. A proxy that wants to read HTTP/3 has to be one of the two ends.

    Recent findings suggest that HTTP proxies use CONNECT to open a tunnel. In HTTP/3, CONNECT still builds a tunnel to a TCP connection (RFC 9114, section 4.4). To tunnel UDP over HTTP there is a different method, CONNECT-UDP (RFC 9298), and most tools and apps do not use it.

    According to recent reports, SOCKS5 can relay UDP. The command is UDP ASSOCIATE (RFC 1928). But many clients never use it. For example, the Chromium network docs say that in Chrome, SOCKSv5 is only used to proxy TCP-based requests and cannot relay UDP (Chromium proxy docs). So pointing a browser at a SOCKS5 proxy does not send its QUIC traffic through that proxy, and you are not testing the QUIC path.

    That leaves two practical ways to get QUIC traffic into a proxy:.

    For how this compares with mitmproxy, see the QUIC interception post.

    Open Proxy, then Redirect, click Add, type the program name (for example curl.exe), leave the action on Proxy, and save. Then click Start Redirect. The status line says Redirecting through the proxy at 127.0.0.1:4444, and the program's TCP and UDP traffic goes through InterceptSuite without changing any setting in the program.

    A rule can also limit the destination hosts and ports. The first matching rule decides, and programs that match no rule are left alone. Remember to trust the InterceptSuite CA on the machine, as in the quick start.

    According to recent reports, curl is a good first test because it is simple and does exactly what you tell it. It needs a build with HTTP/3 support. This example runs on Windows. The curl that ships with Windows (8.21.0 here) does not support HTTP/3: curl -V does not list HTTP3 in its features. So we installed a second curl build that does:.

    In a recent development, the new build (8.23.0) lists HTTP3, ngtcp2 and nghttp3 in curl -V. Check yours the same way before you test, and make sure the new curl is the one that runs (open a new terminal after the install).

    --http3-only makes curl use HTTP/3 and nothing else, so it cannot quietly fall back to TCP. With the Redirect rule on, curl worked without any proxy option and its output revealed HTTP/3 200. No -k was needed, because curl used the Windows trust store, where the InterceptSuite CA is installed.

    In Proxy History the connection appeared as QUIC with host cloudflare-quic.com and ALPN h3:.

    The first client packet (46 bytes) is the request. With the HTTP/3 tab it reads like this:.

    Now turn Intercept ON, run curl again, and change the request while it is held. Replace user-agent: curl/8.23.0 with user-agent: edited-by-proxy and press Forward:.

    Sources indicate that the test site prints back what it saw. The first run says uag=curl/8.23.0. The run with the edit says:.

    So the server got the edited header, and curl never knew. The response is readable too:.

    Look at curl's SETTINGS frame, from the client:.

    Recent findings suggest that QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY: 0 means curl does not use the QPACK dynamic table at all. That is why every curl request is easy to read and edit. We will see the opposite case later.

    Browsers are harder, for two reasons.

    The fix is to start the browser with three flags:.

    In a recent development, is the base64 SHA-256 of the CA's public key. You calculate it from your own CA file:.

    Sources indicate that edge reveals a bar saying the flag is unsupported. That is expected, and it is why you should use a test profile and not your daily one. Close all Edge windows before you start it, or the flags are ignored.

    It has been revealed that with the Redirect rule for msedge.exe on, open https://cloudflare-quic.com/. The page indicates "your browser used HTTP/3":.

    Recent findings suggest that in InterceptSuite the same visit was a QUIC connection with ALPN h3. The request from Edge, decoded by the extension:.

    And the response, with the alt-svc: h3=":443" header the site uses to advertise HTTP/3:.

    In a recent development, the response body here is content-encoding: gzip. The extension decompresses it for display, so the body shows as HTML.

    Edge's SETTINGS are very different from curl's:.

    Edge offers a 64 KB dynamic table and up to 100 blocked streams, so after the first request, Edge can send headers as table references. The QPACK section below explains what that means for reading and editing.

    UDP ASSOCIATE works in two parts.

    The header, from RFC 1928 section 7:.

    The association lives as long as the TCP connection that asked for it. If that TCP connection closes, the UDP association ends (RFC 1928, section 6). This is easy to forget when you write your own client.

    Industry observers note that interceptSuite listens on 127.0.0.1:4444 for SOCKS5 over TCP and 127.0.0.1:4445 for the UDP relay (see the quick start). The reply to UDP ASSOCIATE points to 127.0.0.1:4445.

    Real servers make it hard to see what is going on, so here is a small lab. Both sides use Python and aioquic.

    According to recent reports, the lab client skips certificate checks. That is fine for a lab. A real app must trust the proxy's CA certificate, or it will close the connection when it sees the forged certificate. See Install the CA certificate for that step.

    The lab client sent one request:.

    Here is Proxy History after the client connected, sent requests, and closed.

    According to recent reports, the host column reveals h3.lab.test. That is the server name from the TLS handshake. The ALPN column shows h3. The Protocol column notes QUIC.

    The thing most people do not expect is the number of rows. One request gave 10 entries, not 2. Each row is a chunk of data from one QUIC stream, in the order the proxy saw it. The small ones are all HTTP/3 housekeeping:.

    The client's control stream is three bytes longer than the server's: 0D 01 08 at the end, which is a MAX_PUSH_ID frame.

    Industry observers note that filtering helps a lot here. The filter box understands things like connection_id == 3 and size > 100. The available fields are src_ip, dst_ip, port, direction, protocol, size, modified, connection_id, type, data, host and alpn.

    With the HTTP/3 extension loaded, the control stream entry is shown as text:.

    The 50 00 part is a QUIC variable-length integer. The first two bits (01) say it uses two bytes, and the value is 0x1000, which is 4096. This one matters later, because QPACK's dynamic table is off by default. Both QPACK settings default to zero (RFC 9204, section 5). This server turned it on and allowed 16 blocked streams.

    Recent findings suggest that now the request itself. This is the raw view of the held request packet:.

    Recent findings suggest that you can see the body (user=alice&pw=hunter2), because the body is not compressed. The headers are unreadable. This is QPACK. It is HPACK's cousin for HTTP/3 (RFC 9204), and it does three things:.

    Sources indicate that the HTTP/3 extension from the Extension repository decodes all of this into text. Open the HTTP/3 tab on the same packet:.

    The core of InterceptSuite highlights HTTP/3 as raw bytes. The decoded view comes from this extension. The extension is a normal Python file, and you can read it. Its _decode function parses the QUIC variable-length integers, the HTTP/3 frames, then the QPACK block with the static table and Huffman decoder.

    Turn Intercept ON. By default it holds client-to-server packets. There is also an Intercept response option for the other direction.

    When the client sends its request, the request packet is held and the queue claims 1 packet(s) waiting. Change two things in the HTTP/3 tab: the x-demo header and the body.

    Then press Forward. The server printed this:.

    So the server received the edited request. The client got a normal 200 answer from the server, and its own copy of the request was never changed.

    In Proxy History, the row shows Modified: Yes, and the viewer can show the Original and Edited versions:.

    Two practical points from doing this:.

    Recent findings suggest that the extension does not patch the old bytes. It builds a latest HEADERS frame. From the source, the rules are:.

    This is the part that needs care. So far everything decoded nicely. Now send more requests on the same connection (same headers, different path) and look again.

    The sizes tell the story. Requests 1 and 2 were 122 bytes each. Request 3 was 13 bytes. And at some point, a 114-byte entry demonstrated up on the client's QPACK encoder stream.

    Here are the 13 bytes of request 3, the way they were on the wire:.

    According to recent reports, where are the entries? In the 114-byte entry on the encoder stream. Its first bytes are C0 88 9D 95 E8 1C 6B A4 A8 4F, which is "insert :authority, with a Huffman-coded value" (the value decodes to h3.lab.test). The client sent the long header values once, and every later request only sends numbers. This is a good design. It is also what makes interception harder.

    Look at what the HTTP/3 tab reveals for request 3:.

    According to recent reports, the server's response did the same thing. After a few responses, its header block started using the dynamic table, and the HTTP/3 tab demonstrates the body but only placeholders for two of the headers:.

    There is one more thing to see here. In the capture, the 13-byte request (row 30) arrived before the 114-byte encoder stream entry (row 31). That is allowed by design. QPACK lets a request stream wait ("block") until the inserts it needs have arrived. The server confirmed it could keep up to 16 blocked streams (the QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS setting we saw above). Later a single byte 88 comes back from the server on its decoder stream. That is a Section Acknowledgment for stream 8, which was the third request: the decoder tells the encoder it processed a header block that needed the table (RFC 9204, section 4.4.1).

    So two things follow for a tester:.

    Right-click a row in Proxy History and choose Send to Replay.

    According to recent reports, the session opens with the details filled in: host, port, protocol QUIC, ALPN h3, Newly introduced bidirectional stream, and End stream (FIN) ticked. HTTP/3 request streams are client-started two-way streams, so that is the correct choice. The FIN flag matters because the lab server only answers after it sees the end of the request.

    In the lab the host name h3.lab.test is only a name in the TLS handshake and does not resolve, so change the host to 127.0.0.1. In the HTTP/3 tab, change the path to /admin and x-demo to replayed, then press Send.

    The conversation shows what happened on the wire:.

    The server printed GET /admin x-demo= replayed, and the response JSON highlights "path": "/admin" and "x_demo": "replayed".

    If the edited text leaves a broken header block, Replay sends only a few bytes (25 here) and the server closes the connection:.

    Sources indicate that 0x106 is H3_FRAME_ERROR. RFC 9114 notes that if a stream ends and the last frame on it is cut short, the receiver must treat it as a connection error of this type (RFC 9114, section 7.1). In plain words: the frame header promised more bytes than the stream delivered. If you hand-craft HTTP/3 bytes in the Raw or Hex tab, this is the error you will meet first. It means your frame length does not match your data.

    You can find the current list in the protocol compatibility matrix.

    Related reading: Replay documentation, Proxy History documentation, the HTTP/3 extension source, and Intercepting QUIC and HTTP/3 when mitmproxy isn't enough.
